subsubtopic: SUGGESTED PARTICIPATION OF WORKERS AS SHAREHOLDERS-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion concerning a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
Given the increasing problems faced by the labour market, which is ever more perturbed by unemployment and strikes, since this situation causes considerable prejudice to all those involved in this vicious circle, and since we must at all cost find means of restoring real balance and prosperity in the industry to support effectively our economy which is now faced with severe problems, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard):
That the House of Commons consider forthwith adopting legislation which would enable workers to share in the profits of the industry by holding shares, the revenue of which would be partly deductible for income tax purposes on the same basis as revenue from the stock market, a measure which would immediately and directly stimulate production and reduce the need to strike and would create a healthy climate in the labour market.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE

speechtext: Explain.

subtopic: CRIMINAL CODE
subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PREVENT COURTS OF APPEAL SUBSTITUTING CONVICTION FOR ACQUITTAL BY JURY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to supplement Bill C-71, presently before the House, and delete the provision in the Criminal Code which allows the court of appeal to supersede the verdict of a jury. It would apply to victims now serving terms of imprisonment because they were convicted by a court of appeal after being acquitted by a jury. On passage of this bill, any such victim or victims would be released.
The right hon. gentleman from Prince Albert (Mr. Die-fenbaker) has introduced a bill similar in intent and there is also government legislation before the House to amend the Criminal Code in the way I suggest. However, neither bill provides for the release of any victim or victims presently serving sentences of imprisonment. At present, only one person in Canada is in prison because of conviction by the court of appeal. He is Dr. Henry Morgentaler. This public bill would apply to that individual, he being the only person in Canada caught in such circumstances.

speakeroldname: Hon. Barney Danson (Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: HOUSING
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMKNT OF FEDERAL ACTION PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to outline to hon. members the federal housing action program, a series of measures designed to produce one million new housing units over the next four years, with a 1976 target of 235,000. The commitment of the federal government is to ensure production of the kind of good quality housing that lower and middle income Canadians need and can afford and, through these measures, to dampen inflation in the housing sector and stimulate economic growth and the creation of employment opportunities.
In order to achieve these objectives, the government will require private lending institutions to direct mortgage financing to lower and moderately priced new housing. In 1976, this will require an additional $750 million, for a total new housing market of $8 billion. The government will establish a monitoring committee to ensure this target is met. The government will require private lending institutions to restrict their low down payment-high ratio- lending to NHA regional loan limits, and these loan limits will be held down consistent with our price guidelines. We will make the Assisted Home Ownership Program- AHOP-available to any Canadian household of two or more people wanting to buy moderately-priced housing and to keep their monthly payments equivalent to those of an 8 per cent mortgage. The requirement of having at least one child is removed, enabling young couples to purchase a home before starting their family.
For people with children who need help to keep their monthly payments under 25 per cent of their income, grants, which are now a maximum of $600 a year, are increased to $750. For others, assistance will be in the form of a loan which will be interest-free for at least the first five years, and repayable with interest after that time or when the house is sold or refinanced upwards. The loan will be sufficient to cover the difference between market interest rates and interest at 8 per cent.
We will stimulate increased production of moderately-priced rental accommodation. The assisted rental program will make interest-free loans available to builders who will create rental housing at rents controlled by CMHC during the period of support of up to 15 years. Maximum annual loans to builders will be increased from $900 to $1,200 per unit to compensate for recent interest rate increases and to encourage supply. These loans will be recoverable. In addition, we will ask the House to approve continuation of the special capital cost allowance provisions for non-principal business rental entrepreneurs until December 31, 1977.
To improve the liquidity of mortgages as an investment, the government will make the federal Mortgage Exchange Corporation operational by April 1, 1976. To make moderate-cost housing development more attractive to municipalities, the government will make $1,000 per unit grants available to municipalities which approve medium density housing within regional AHOP and assisted rental price limits. The government will now make loans and grants available to municipalities for water treatment facilities and mains where they are needed to open up land for housing, on the same basis as assistance presently given to

municipalities under the sewage treatment program for sanitary and storm sewers.
The eight-point program I have just enunciated, Mr. Speaker, is designed to fill the real needs of Canadians who are not suitably housed at the moment by providing them with access to housing they can afford. This will stimulate employment in the construction industry by creating 32,000 additional jobs in 1976. The entire four-year program involves more than a million man-years of employment.
One of the very real advantages of this program is that it directs more private capital into the moderately-priced residential mortgage market utilizing a minimum amount of taxpayers' dollars. This allows the federal government to direct its resources to Canadians in greatest need, such as senior citizens, native people, the handicapped, and others who are socially and economically deprived.
I would also like to inform hon. members that at the federal-provincial housing ministers' conference earlier today, I urged the provinces to institute rent controls consistent with the federal government's commitment to contain inflation and support new housing construction and, indeed, received that assurance. I have also asked my provincial colleagues to requires those lending institutions under provincial jurisdiction to increase their mortgage lending in line with the federal guidelines. I received that assurance.
I believe hon. members will agree that these long-range measures will enable the construction industry to marshall its resources for economic and competitive production in order to meet the most pressing needs of those Canadians who are finding difficulty acquiring adequate housing at reasonable cost under today's difficult conditions. I will be introducing legislation in the House in the very near future for the consideration of hon. members. Subject to legislative approval, the measures will be effective as of today.

We all recall his prediction of a minimum of 210,000 starts this year. The record to date is 12 per cent off target. We all recall the $1 billion of private funds that AHOP was to attract for mortgages. The record to date is $66 million. In his statement, the minister mentioned $750 million for new housing starts. If we were to be generous regarding that prediction and work it out, it would come to perhaps
25.000	units per year, or 100,000 units in four years-some
900.000	short of the target the minister mentioned. I am sure the minister will want to elaborate on this shortfall. Perhaps once again he will fall back on AHOP as the catch-all for everything he cannot determine otherwise.
Some of the measures which the minister put forward today are those which we on this side of the House have advocated for some time. We strongly pressed for legislation which would provide assistance for municipalities to increase the amount of serviced land available. I am glad to see that certain aspects of this have been dealt with. We have repeatedly urged the government to set up the Federal Mortgage Exchange Corporation. I remind the minister that the legislation enabling him to do so has been on the books for three years.
I find several basic shortcomings in the minister's program. First, these measures will not stimulate provision of the amount of mortgage funding required to finance the supply of new housing which is so vitally needed if the inflationary aspect of housing is to be reduced. New money to the extent of $750 million is not the answer to that deficiency. Second, there is nothing in the statement to deal with the major problem presented by the high interest rates which hundreds of thousands of Canadians have been obliged to assume in the last year-a burden which will almost certainly continue to weigh heavily for many years to come. Nowhere is there any indication that the government is prepared to take measures which come to grips with the fact that well over 30 per cent of the income of these individuals goes into financing home buying. Nowhere is there any sign of relief for those who are caught by high interest rates.
Then, again, apart from a brief reference to the minister's action in urging his provincial counterparts to institute rent controls, there is no indication in the statement as to the form and level of rent control the federal government considers appropriate to its over-all restraint program.
Finally, the program fails to deal with the necessity for continuity in housing policy. Instead, emphasis has been placed on unilateral housing programs by the federal government. Scarcely any reference is made to co-operation with the provinces, something which must play a major part in the direction of housing. Thus, I would say there is nothing original about these measures. We have had stepped-up programs, expanded programs and resurrected programs, but still no recognition by the government that adequate shelter is a basic, ongoing right of all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, the New Democratic Party feels that the measures announced by the minister today are unimpressive and will do very little to solve the housing crisis in Canada. In fact, they constitute a typical attempt to appear to be doing something very dramatic while actually doing very little. One cannot deny that the measures will have some effect on the housing problems, but they will not strike at the main problems of
Housing
housing today, namely, the high cost of land and high interest rates.
I was rather impressed with the statement by the minister when he said the target for the next four years would be one million homes, because as I recall, Mr. Speaker, back in 1970 the same government announced its target as being one million homes over five years. It may be said that they achieved one million homes over five years, but in achieving that target we have experienced the worst crisis in housing Canadians have ever known. That is because the government has used the same old approaches, and it is these approaches the minister announced today. We really need five main features: first, a steady flow of funds; second, a target for homes of a certain type; third, low interest rates; fourth, low land costs and assistance with the servicing of land; and fifth, rental guidelines.
With regard to a steady flow of funds, the minister stated we would require the financial institutions to direct a certain amount of their moneys to mortgage financing. We in the New Democratic Party have recommended this for a long time, and it is high time the minister took such an initiative. But the success of this initiative will depend upon the legislation the minister brings forth in parliament, because the financial institutions have been playing a game of yo-yo with housing in respect of their financial commitment in the past. Unless the minister is direct and forceful in the legislation, very little will be accomplished.
The target of one million homes over four years was mentioned. This will require the close co-operation of the federal government with the provincial governments and the municipalities. It really calls for a strong emphasis upon public housing, more especially rental public housing. It also requires an emphasis on co-operative and nonprofit housing. Mr. Speaker, may I remind you that all the public housing we have today amounts to less than 2 per cent of our total housing starts. This indicates the necessity of action by the government.
To achieve the minister's target of one million homes, the minister has adopted a pandering or bended-knee approach to the builders, developers and financial institutions. For example, there are to be interest-free loans to builders who will create rental housing controlled by CMHC up to 15 years, and increased loans on rental units from $900 to $1,200 which the minister says is to compensate for recent increases and to encourage supply. Mr. Speaker, this is a rerun of the minister's legislation of 1974 on private, limited dividend housing where he gave builders generous interest rates and agreements for five years. All he is doing is rehashing and renewing in attempting to encourage builders to build more housing. What is needed is public, limited dividend housing, that is, public housing-more especially on the rental side-and increases in co-operative and non-co-operative housing where there is control over rents, repairs and services.
The minister also mentioned that he would prescribe lower interest rates in connection with Assisted Home Ownership Programs. The main item which is missing from the anti-inflation legislation is control of interest rates. This is what is really needed, because we see ever-escalating interest rates across the board in Canada. This is the type of action which has to be taken, because interest rates are the main component in the rising cost of

housing. I am not impressed with the suggestion of putting into line the Federal Mortgage Exchange Corporation by April, 1976. It will do nothing to bring down interest rates; it will just be doing what CMHC has done in the past. I am impressed with the minister's suggestion that there be grants to municipalities for water treatment and water mains, but the success of this initiative will depend upon the amount of funds allocated.
Finally, the minister told us in his statement that he had urged the provincial ministers of housing to implement rent controls along the guidelines set forth in the antiinflation legislation. May I say that I do not think this is sufficient. What has to be achieved is a roll-back of rents. Rent review boards should be set up. It is not sufficient to tell landlords that they may increase their rents by only a certain percentage, because one has no idea of the increased costs they have experienced. I thought the minister would adopt the suggestion of the New Democratic Party in Ontario, roll back interest rates to January of this year and, at the most, allow a 6 per cent increase. Further increases by landlords should have to be justified before a rent review board.
There appears to be an absence of leadership in this legislation and there is an absence of meaningful programs. This will result in a continuance of the serious housing problems we have today.

This is not for direct investment to individuals, but it makes the mortgage instrument far more liquid and far more attractive to investors, particularly non-traditional investors. Massive pools of capital are available through pension funds, for instance, and I am sure my hon. friends in the NDP would not want to see them take interest rates lower than they can get. So it makes it a more attractive instrument in that respect. It also makes far more attractive the mortgage investment corporations which had legislation passed at the same time. It really creates a secondary market for mortgages. It will create a lot more activity. subtopic: HOUSING

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the minister has not answered my question which was as follows: will the ordinary individual, the one who makes investments, have the chance to invest in this Federal Mortgage Exchange Corporation set up to build housing? speakerposition: Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: HOUSING
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMKNT OF FEDERAL ACTION PROGRAM
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker, it is actually a secondary market, a sort of wholesaling operation for mortgages so that people can buy mortgages knowing they are liquid, and they can resell to the Federal Mortgage Exchange Corporation; or, indeed, they can buy from that corporation. In CMHC alone we have a substantial portfolio of mortgages which can be used and wholesaled there. So it is not a direct investment for the individual, although it makes investment for the individual much more attractive whether he or she does it through conventional channels or not.
I want to reiterate the connection with regard to the mortgage investment corporation which is a tax conduit for small investors who want to invest in mortgages. It is specifically for mortgages and the corporation taxes; full benefits flow through to the individual and it becomes a much more attractive investment for household mortgages. It should attract capital from many sources. I mentioned pension funds specifically because they have not been active in this field. This proposal makes it a much more attractive field for them to get into.

subtopic: HOUSING
subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMKNT OF FEDERAL ACTION PROGRAM

November 3, 1975

subtopic: ANSWERS GIVEN TO QUESTIONS PLACED ON ORDER PAPER
ANSWERS GIVEN TO QUESTIONS PLACED ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order at the first opportunity in respect of order paper question No. 3119, and the answer thereto. The question itself was as follows:
Did the Prime Minister say at the opening of the new Mirabel airport: "The Torontonians will be down on their knees" and, if so
(a)	for what reason did he make the statement
(b)	what is the full meaning of the statement
(c)	was it meant as a public affront to the people of Ontario, and
Toronto in particular?
The answer given by the government was as follows:
See Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, Citation 171 (e).
This citation, at page 147, states that a question, oral or written, must not seek, for purposes of argument, information on a matter of past history. It is my view, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) have recently been using references from Beauchesne's that do not accurately apply to the questions involved and this, I submit, is a case in point. I bring this matter up, Mr. Speaker, because I firmly believe that if the procedure is allowed to continue, a mockery will be made of the right of members of this House to put questions to the government.
At the opening of Mirabel airport, the Prime Minister made a very serious statement: "Torontonians will be down here on their knees". As a result, it would seem to me that there is no legitimate reason, nor any ruling in Beauchesne's, which prohibits a member of this House from questioning the Prime Minister on such a statement. Accordingly, I asked the Prime Minister for what reason he made this statement and I also asked him the full meaning of the statement. In reply, a section of Beauchesne's is quoted which prohibits seeking an answer for "purposes of argument".
I respectfully submit, Mr. Speaker, that the question had nothing to do with "purposes of argument". It certainly did have something to do with the right of a member to receive clarification of a statement by the Prime Minister at least in so far as whether it is the policy of his government to create a situation where Torontonians will be running to Mirabel to get down on their knees in front of him, and to know the reasons for such a statement, the meaning of such a statement and, in effect, whether or not it represents government policy. Now, this question also was rejected by the government by the use of a further quotation from Beauchesne's.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANSWERS GIVEN TO QUESTIONS PLACED ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Order, please. I do not want to restrict the hon. member in raising what may appear to him to be a point of order. The fact of the matter is that it is well known, without the citations from Beauschesne's to which he has referred, that the rules provide no obligation to make an answer to questions put by hon. members. That citation and that precedent certainly are well known to all members of the House. Whether or not an hon. member is satisfied with the answer he receives or the reason for not receiving an answer, that may be a subject of debate or
Point of Order-Mr. Cossitt
comment which the hon. member may wish to make at the appropriate time.
I am simply saying to the hon. member that unless he can depart in some way from his present line of argument, he will be unable to satisfy the Chair that there is a point of order involved in the points he has.

subtopic: ANSWERS GIVEN TO QUESTIONS PLACED ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I quite agree, as I was about to point out in this statement, that a minister is not obliged to answer a question, nor is he obliged to answer a question in such a way that I, as a member of the opposition-or any other member of this House-have a right to question it in so far as the substance of the answer is concerned.
But I think we are dealing here with a different point. I am trying to illustrate that it is not a case of my disagreeing with the answer, as an individual member. Rather, it is a case of the rules being used in such a way as to be a misuse of the rules. If I could continue for a moment, I think I can illustrate the point I am trying to make. For instance, it was also rejected on the ground, quoting again from Beauchesne's, that it is "information on matter of past history".
I find it impossible to see how the conclusion can be arrived at that such a statement by the Prime Minister, made only a day or so before I put the question, has already become something of an historical nature. Indeed, if the government is going to invoke this particular section of Beauchesne's, then it becomes impossible for a member of this House to question anything the Prime Minister says anywhere in so far as it concerns government policy, because apparently this government has now elevated all utterances of the Prime Minister to the historical level.
I would like to make one further reference to the answer given to another question, namely, question No. 2,328 which asks for details concerning the cost to taxpayers of the trip made to London, Paris, and Brussels for a period of 36 days by Mr. Michael Pitfield who is now secretary to the cabinet and clerk of the Privy Council. The government answered, properly and correctly, that the cost of the trip to the taxpayers was a certain number of dollars. It answered, properly and correctly, as to who was the person authorizing the trip. But the third part of the question, asking in what ways the taxpayers benefited from the expenditure of public funds, was ruled out again by quoting Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, citation 171 (b), which reads "trivial, vague, or meaningless".
I submit this is, again, an example of the misuse of the rules of the House. If Mr. Pitfield travels to Europe for 36 days at public expense, then it seems to me a member of the House has the privilege of asking in what ways such a trip was of benefit to Canadian taxpayers, who paid for it. It is a misapplication of citation 171(b) of Beauchesne's because there is certainly nothing trivial about expenditures of public funds by a public servant, there is nothing vague about directly requesting to know in what way the taxpayers benefited from such expenditures, and for the government to further imply that the question is meaningless is, I believe, an insult to the taxpayers who paid for the trip.

Point of Order-Mr. Cossitt
In conclusion, if the Prime Minister is going to make unclear statements about the people of a city such as Toronto, if the Prime Minister's high ranking officials in the civil service are going to spend public money to travel hither and yon, then I submit there is nothing to prohibit a member of this House questioning such matters and stating that the government has started a dangerous program of misusing precedents of the House to block an answer to these questions.
Finally, I fully realize-as you so rightly pointed out a moment ago, sir-that under the rules of the House, ministers are not obliged to answer questions. I also realize that a member of the House has no recourse against the substance of an answer to a question with which he disagrees. But I believe it is a legitimate point of order when the government misuses the rules of the House to protect itself from having to explain the truth to the elected representatives of the people, and if this process continues I hope that the Chair will then take the matter under examination.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: ANSWERS GIVEN TO QUESTIONS PLACED ON ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Order, please. The hon. member has raised a point of order concerning answers made by the government to questions, and has already pointed out-as I said a moment ago-that there is no obligation upon the government to answer questions put on the order paper. The Chair will examine the argument put forward by the hon. member to see whether in fact there has been a misuse of the precedents in the answer that has been given. But it seems to the Chair, at the outset, that two things are clear. The first is that if there is anything wrong with making an improper allusion to precedents in failing to make an answer, it is difficult to know if it would establish a point of order, because this gets us back to the point of whether there is an obligation to answer the question in the first place.
In the second place, the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Cossitt), in addition to seeking information also sought the opinion of the government on whether taxpayers were going to benefit from a certain trip, and what was the meaning of the statement made by the Prime Minister. In both these cases there is certainly ground, not so much for information but for an expression of opinion, for a description or for an impression of the person who happens to be answering the question. The difficulty into which I do not want to enter is that since there is no obligation on the government to answer questions, there is a tendency on the part of the Chair to allow wide latitude in questions that hon. members put on the order paper.
If we are to be extremely technical about one side of the matter, it is obvious the Chair will have the obligation to be extremely technical about the other side and will have to take a firm hand in ruling out those questions which are in some ways out of order. The Chair does intervene and examines the questions in a cursory way to try to weed out those that are obviously out of order. I do not think hon. members would want the Chair to intervene frequently and take a hard line in respect of questions put on the order paper, but that might be the logical result of becoming too technical on both sides.
In any case, I will endeavour to examine the arguments put forward by the hon. member to see whether or not a valid point of order exists.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT

speechtext: The House resumed from Wednesday, October 29, consideration of the motion of Mr. Andras that Bill C-69, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate on Bill C-69, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, has continued to give rise, since we adjourned the debate, to many comments, in both written and electronic media, and no doubt many Canadians have continued to take interest in this vital question.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to resume the discussion this afternoon on the provisions of the bill which exclude persons who are 65 from unemployment insurance benefits. The act through which unemployment insurance was adopted was intended, essentially, to achieve two objectives: the first, to protect the worker's income; the second, to encourage the unemployed to reintegrate the work force.
The Unemployment Insurance Commission learned from experience in the last few years that a large number of workers, 65 or over, do not make the effort, do not give themselves the trouble of finding and keeping a job, that workers in other categories are required to do. I have mentioned before in this House that the inquiries of Statistics Canada in past years have proved that at least half of the unemployed of 65 or more who collect unemployment insurance make no effort, or no visible effort to go back to work and that, as a corollary to this fact, civil servants and unemployment insurance inspectors have quite a hard time applying, as strictly as they should, the rules governing the efforts and steps which a temporarily unemployed worker should make to go back to work.
So we have a difficult situation where, on the one side, it is extremely difficult for controllers to force a worker of 65 to take the necessary steps to find employment and on the other side, where a number of workers who are 65 or more are not really willing to reintegrate the labour market, and this is lamentable.
The solution put forward in the legislation is fairly simple. It is aimed at excluding simply all workers who are 65 or more. The reasons for this exclusion stem mainly from measures passed by the government in recent years, and more particularly since 1952, since the adoption of the old age security plan. Now, we note this astonishing and satisfying fact, Mr. Speaker, that the retired persons, people who are 65 or more, have up to now been able to face the rise in the cost of living thanks to the pensions they could get from the old age security plan, the guaranteed income supplement, the Quebec Pension Plan and the Canada Pension Plan. These different programs seem to have been clearly sufficient to maintain the purchasing power of retired people, of those who are 65 or more.
I do not invent this statement, Mr. Speaker, nor do I take it from government documents whose credibility could certainly be challenged. One could surely question the
November 3, 1975

arguments of the government if I asserted, on the strenght of governmental studies, that Canadian pensioners, citizens of 65 or over, have been able up to now to meet the cost of living increase. That statement, Mr. Speaker, is extracted from a study by the firm Towers, Perrin, Foster and Crosby, which has a branch in New York and has done a similar study on the American market.
It is clearly indicated in this study that higher old age security pensions and allowances, the indexing of allowances, and increases in the guaranteed income supplement allow the Canadian pensioner to benefit from income support which puts him in a position nearly 100 per cent better than in 1952. Indeed the financial position of senior citizens has greatly improved in Canada thanks to the adjustments the federal government made through the Quebec Pension Plan and the Canada Pension Plan. When the Canada Pension Plan was introduced by the federal government in 1952, a pensioner aged 70 was entitled to a monthly allowance of $40.
Those who were the first to benefit under this plan are now entitled, provided of course they are still alive, to $125.76 a month, that is 214 per cent above what they received in 1952. From 1952 to 1975, the increase in consumer prices has been 101.3 per cent. Which means, Mr. Speaker, that between 1952 and 1975, on the whole, the position of senior citizens, the position of those Canadians who have received old age pensions has significantly improved. Therefore the real purchasing power of the Canadian pensioner has jumped 50 per cent, since what he could buy in 1952 for $40 costs about $80 in 1975.
The survey by Towers, Perrin, Foster and Crosby on the comparative increases in the prices of rent, food, clothing and related needs, infers that not only did the first years of the Canada Pension Plan allow people to catch up with the rise in the cost of living, but also paved the way for improved living standards. So the basic pension which amounted to $40 a month in 1952 rose to $55 six years later and to $75 after the 1963 amendments. In other words, since the indexation of old age security, the claimant, the Canadian pensioner, gets a revenue supplement which allows him to live twice better than the 1952 pensioner. But since the establishment of the Quebec Pension Plan and the Canada Pension Plan, other benefits are paid, besides old age security.
The findings of this study on the American market are nearly identical. Indeed, the pensions paid to the American pensioner have been increasing steadily and show that the current revenue of the American pensioner is in line with what the Canadian pensioner gets. However, Mr. Speaker, anomalies still continue to exist which allow us to think that the proposed amendments in Bill C-69 are not enough. Indeed, the calculation of the income supplement as done by the Quebec Department of Social Affairs indicates a basic inequality.
Indeed, instead of taking the special needs supplement, the amounts of $219 a month paid out as old age pensions and the guaranteed income supplement as a base, the Quebec Department of Social Affairs takes $195 as a basic figure and adds the additional amounts which may be calculated for special needs. That means that every Canadian pensioner who gets the guaranteed income supplement in addition to the old age pension is relieved of an
Unemployment Insurance Act
amount of $28 for all special needs, or for any test of special needs he can prove to appropriate institutions. Thus, a retired Canadian who lives in Quebec and must claim additional needs in terms of medical care, in terms of related care, must have his guaranteed income supplement cut by $28 before he can get an additional amount.
The situations to which this calculation can lead give staggering results. For example, a couple aged 80 who get $349 a month as their pension and guaranteed income, the husband being blind and an amputee, is not entitled to a supplement from the Quebec Department of Social Affairs before they spend virtually all allowances they get to support their primary needs. I think, Mr. Speaker, that if the income supplement is to be reviewed, if the legislation affecting the retired is to be reviewed, those anomalies that exist now in respect of related needs should be corrected.
Mr. Speaker, another anomaly still continues to exist and it was corrected in part by federal legislation. It has to do with that application of the means test to people who come under the Quebec Pension Plan. In a previous amendment the Parliament of Canada did away with what the legal jargon called the means test. At the present time, anyone who applies for a pension under the Canada Pension Plan does not have to submit to a means test to get a pension, to get the maximum pension. This government, this Parliament, are the ones which in the last few months did away with the application of a criterion that no longer corresponded with the true situation of Canadian pensioners.
Now, the Quebec Pension Plan still provides for a means test which contributes to perpetuate this inequality added to the other needs I mentioned earlier.
Consequently, Mr. Speaker, if the Canadian pensioners throughout the country are to be on an equal footing, we must make sure that all the income support provisions of the various programs give similar results.
Some colleagues have pointed out that the number of claimants now eligible for benefits as of January 1, 1976 would total from 20,000 to 25,000 and that to this cumulative number would be added from 10,000 to 15,000 claimants during 1976. This means, Mr. Speaker, that if the provisions of the bill were passed word for word by the House, some 40,000 Canadian claimants would not be covered by unemployment insurance.
Mr. Speaker, I mentioned at the beginning of my remarks that the object of unemployment insurance was to protect the income of workers. Now, the amendments before the House are designed to deprive a 65 year-old worker of the protection of his right to work. It is not true, as pointed out by the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Fortin), that the bill is aimed at depriving people of 65 of the right to work. I think that no Canadian law could, in a free economy such as ours, abolish the individual right to work.
This bill removes rather the protection of the right to work. Now, we must ask ourselves at this stage, following the inquiries made by Statistics Canada, whether those figures are sufficient to prompt us to stop protecting the right to work of workers between 65 and 70, a right which was recognized in the 1971 bill.

November 3, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
Some editorial writers and some previous speakers have shown that the philosophy of most government programs now designed for older persons aims at integrating them into community activities. The budget of programs such as New Horizons has tripled in the last two years, precisely with a view to integrating Canadian pensioners into community activities. These programs have been very successful, and nobody would think of excluding from them citizens of 55 or 50.
The eligibility criteria has been greatly extended and a large number of Canadians nearing 50 take advantage of these programs.
It would be illogical at this time when there is an attempt to integrate pensioners into community activities, to exclude without exception the pensioners who wish to remain in the labour force.
Undeniably a person who has reached age 65 and quit his job, either because the clauses of a collective agreement force him to retire or because, being 67 years old he has decided to retire, cannot logically be still subsidized by Canadian taxpayers through a plan aimed first of all at protecting the right to work of people who do not want to be on the labour market.
On the other hand it would be illogical to exclude out of hand all citizens aged 65 who still have the energy, the capability and most of all are available for work. There are Canadian businesses whose manpower reserves are mostly people over 60. How would they be affected if the pensionable age was lowered to 60? My hon. colleagues in the opposition have often pointed out that lowering the age of eligibility for old age security would result in freeing a certain number of jobs and therefore absorbing some unemployed whose number is much too great in the present economic conditions.
I believe there is a middle course that would allow us to maintain within our laws the protection of the right to work for all pensioners or 65 year old people. I think that a Canadian of 65 should have the choice either to remain in the labour force and keep paying unemployment insurance contributions or simply to opt out of the unemployment insurance plan. Our legislation has never given the Canadian worker the option of withdrawing from the unemployment insurance system. It was a compulsory universal plan which was supposed to apply to all Canadian workers without exception.
The government proposal aims at excluding from the scheme all citizens aged 65. It does not give them the choice, the option to continue receiving benefits and paying premiums. If it is to remain an insurance scheme, I feel the unemployment insurance plan must allow citizens aged 65 to opt out if they want to withdraw permanently from the labour force. So, a person of 65 could notify the Unemployment Insurance Commission of his intention to opt out of the unemployment insurance scheme and to collect, as provided under the bill, a three-week severance benefit as compensation until his readjustment under the various income support programs I mentioned earlier.
Thus, we would end up, Mr. Speaker, with a plan which I feel would maintain for workers of 65 the incentives to return to the labour marked needed by the Canadian

economy. It would also allow the Unemployment Insurance Commission and plan to unload a number of workers who, at 65, decide and really wish not to go back to work, and who anyway do not want to make the effort and take the steps required to find a job under difficult economic circumstances.
I would therefore suggest to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration, who proved he is really open-minded by introducing at least five amendments which substantially improve the unemployment insurance program, that he consider giving workers of 65 the opportunity to advise the Commission that they want to opt out of the plan and to receive three weeks of benefit provided for in the government proposal, and allowing those who want to remain in the labour force to continue to contribute, with all the responsibilities and obligations this implies. And if, unfortunately, as a result of the severe controls which must be made by UIC inspectors and officials, the conclusion was reached that those workers are not taking the steps nor submitting to the controls provided for in the act, we would have no other alternative than to disentitle them to receive benefits payable to workers under 65.
I feel that to provide this option under the legislation would show that we acknowledge that the worker of 65 is still making a useful and effective contribution to the Canadian economy and would remove the disincentive to work that other pieces of legislation and government programs seek specifically to compensate.

Mr. Speaker, the bill we are debating is one of the many dubious pieces of legislation following from the document tabled last June which the previous minister of finance was pleased to call the budget. That budget proved to be a launching pad. Indeed, it should have been called that in the first place. The previous minister of finance who introduced that budget has since been launched to the middle benches on the other side and is the latest of the long list of cabinet ministers who have played the role of sacrificial lamb as the government blunders from crisis to crisis. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) should have made the exfinance minister a gift of the budget when he made his grand exit, in the way some companies give retiring employees a gold watch. We could then have made a fresh start from square one. We might even have offered the services of our able finance critic-on a consulting basis, of course. This government is all too familiar with the role of the consultant. There are more consultants on the present government's payroll than there have been at any time in Canada's history.
The Liberal government of Quebec seems to have learned a lesson about hiring consultants from the federal Liberal government, or possibly it was the other way around. According to the reports now being circulated about consulting services for the Olympic site in Montreal, the consulting bill alone on the first phase of the project will amount to about $23 million. Of course, there is the matter of the criminal nonsense concerning the payment of more than $30 million to the architect of the domed stadium at the Olympic site.
November 3, 1975

I point out, Mr. Speaker, that members of this House, whatever party they represent, have a very personal stake in this proposed legislation to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act. From my own experience, I say that the average member devotes more time and effort to solving UIC cases in the constituency than to all other types of problems put together. This should give some idea of the magnitude of the problem both with respect to the unreasonably high rate of unemployment in Canada and the difficulty experienced by many legitimate claimants in getting their UIC benefits.
Part of the problem in getting UIC claims settled stems from the fact that there are just too many professional UIC cheats. These people tie up the employees of the local UIC offices, drain the UIC fund and force sympathetic UIC employees to adopt a cynical attitude to all claimants, legitimate and otherwise. A couple of years ago the government announced the hiring of an army of ex-policemen, private eyes and other investigative personnel to track down UIC cheats and restore some credibility to the UIC program. Since then I have not heard anything about the project and I have to assume that it has been a dismal failure; also, that most, if not all, those people are now drawing their own unemployment insurance benefits.
Let me stress that the problems we encounter with the Unemployment Insurance Commission are not with the employees of the local UIC offices. My staff and I have always found these people to be courteous, co-operative an helpful. Employees in local offices appear to be just as anxious as the rest of us to see that the program works the way it should, and they are sympathetic to the plight of legitimate claimants. I find that they are also diligent in their efforts to identify and to apprehend the chisellers.
It is interesting to note that UIC employees, especially in local offices, are not awed or overwhelmed by inquiries directed to them by members of parliament. They are responsive and courteous, do not hesitate to point out that some cases of overpayment raise on the basis of false information supplied by claimants, and that the money must be repaid. By the same token, they will not hesitate to admit an error on the part of the UIC office and will often make payments to claimants to cover periods where disentitlements were imposed in error. Mr. Speaker, we cannot fault employees in UIC offices for the failure of the program to work the way it was intended and the way we must ensure it will work.
In order to find the culprits responsible for one of the most expensive boondoggles in the long list of blunders committed by this government, we must go to the top of the bureaucracy and the top of the political ladder. That is where we must go if we are to find those responsible and at the heart of the appalling mess in which the UIC today finds itself. We knew three or four years ago that the Unemployment Insurance Commission was mismanaging the UIC program, and we were alerted to the fact some incompetent people were parachuted into senior positions in the commission, people who had failed miserably in their former positions.
We knew as long ago as 1971 that the government did not intend to take steps to replace the incompetents in the commission. The Prime Minister tried to restore some semblance of order in the UIC house by using his majority
Unemployment Insurance Act
to railroad through parliament a bill which would remove the ceiling on UIC pay-outs. In that way UIC could continue in the same old way and would have an abundance of money under which it could hide its inefficiency and blunders. The Prime Minister also undertook to make up any deficits in the unemployment insurance fund while unemployment remained in excess of 4 per cent of the labour force. Under this new legislation, the Prime Minister has raised his sights to a figure of 5 per cent. In other words, he is prepared to accept 5 per cent to 6 per cent unemployment as equivalent to full employment. This only compounds the travesty of looking upon unemployed Canadians as numbers in a set of filing cards.
The mere idea of 800,000 unemployed Canadians being an acceptable rate of misery and deprivation in our country is deplorable. When it becomes a policy of government, that government does not have the moral right to remain in power. I wonder whether the government would have the courage to go to the electorate on a platform that contained such a policy, combined with a history of flipflopping on the question of inflation.
Just over a year ago, the Prime Minister spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on television and radio time telling the Canadian people that the Conservative proposal for price and income controls would not work. Today we have the most restrictive and wide ranging controls in peacetime history. I invite the Prime Minister to call an election and campaign on those two issues.
It is typical of this government to try to save money by cutting back on the level of benefits paid to the legitimately unemployed. Surely the Prime Minister knows that cutting the level of benefits will only add to the misery of those families without their accustomed level of income. To say that the difference will be made up with family benefits is complete and utter nonsense. There are thousands of families with one or two children. There are others with no children, especially young and middle-aged couples. In some cases, a couple that has already raised their children will need to have an adequate income if the breadwinner loses his job through no fault of his own.
For years the Prime Minister and his cabinet have been doing everything in their power to discourage business and industrial expansion, the very lifeblood of employment, especially with regard to the creation of new jobs required every year based on additions to the labour force. It is as though the government is swinging a double-edged sword at the working people of this country, discouraging expansion in job-creating areas, raising the premium for unemployment insurance and then cutting back on UIC benefits. There is a classic case of confusion and indecision if ever I saw one.
To get back to the question of abuses of the unemployment insurance program, I would like to deal for a few minutes with the remarks of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) concerning people who quit their jobs and those who refuse employment when it is offered to them. I accept the fact that when as many as 250,000 people quit their jobs in a given year, it is a serious matter, one that all of us are anxious to see explained and one we would like to see cleared up. The minister did not

Unemployment Insurance Act
have a breakdown on that enormous figure, but I have to assume that he would not have given the figure if it did not represent people who had made application for UIC benefits. The minister did not say how many of those people quit their jobs because they could not continue because of health or other legitimate reasons. He did not say how many quit because their working conditions were intolerable and they could not take it any longer.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, the minister simply threw that figure at us as though he was using it to justify the drastic provisions of this bill, the main purpose of which is to make it look as though the government is deeply concerned about its expenditures. The same might be said about the figure of 26,000 jobs refused by people who were drawing UIC benefits in the period noted by the minister. How many of these people actually turned down jobs for which they were qualified? How many of those jobs required the people to uproot their families and move to job sites hundreds of miles from their place of residence? What I and, I am sure, my colleagues would like to know is whether the minister was actually giving us exact figures of those who sought to abuse the UIC program, or whether in fact there were extenuating circumstances in any or most of the figures he gave us.
I am aware of certain cases that fit into this category. It makes me wonder whether some of them, mostly wives, should be entitled. In some cases, a husband and wife work in the city, the husband with a much better job, or he decides to go into business for himself in a rural area. The family moves with him and the wife then immediately applies for unemployment insurance benefits.
All of us are interested in shutting out the cheaters and the rip-offs in the UIC program. We also want to see better and faster service for those who are legitimate claimants for UIC benefits. However, Mr. Speaker, if the government is simply throwing large numbers at us in the hope that we will get alarmed and demand an immediate crackdown on UIC claimants, across the board, they do not have a hope. We want honest figures and we want an honest appraisal of the problem of UIC cheating. It would also be helpful for us to know to what extent legitimate claimants are being penalized in the government's attempts to uncover and apprehend UIC cheaters.
The Minister of Manpower and Immigration said that the government hopes to collect an additional $490 million for the UIC fund through the provisions of this bill. If that money is to be raised by penalizing those who are already burdened with the premiums for the UIC program, and by reducing the benefits to those legitimate unemployed people who qualify for benefits, then the $490 million will have to be considered under the heading of ill-gotten gains.
Considering the way in which the present government throws money around, and considering the amount of money wasted in inefficiency and bungling by this government, I cannot accept such measures as are contained in Bill C-69 to enable the government to raise more money. Let them clean house, bring some order and efficiency into the UIC upper echelons, and cut out some of the appalling waste in other government programs that serve no other purpose than to reward Liberal losers and hacks and the mere party faithful. Let us save money in that way; then we will not have to keep squeezing it out of the overbur-

dened workers of Canada and we will not have to raise it by penalizing those who are the legitimate beneficiaries of government programs.
Recently the Ottawa Journal ran a story on the bill under the headline "Workers to bear heavier UIC load". Under the new legislation, maximum premiums for employees would rise immediately from $1.40 per week to $1.70 and could go as high as $3.40 by 1977. Employers premiums will rise from the present $2.40 to $2.80 and, again, in 1977 could be $4.80. The minister says that the new regulations will require employees and employers to pay $490 million into the UIC fund and will allow the federal government to save $600 million in 1976. That is certainly a switch. It is a shabby way for the government to create the impression that it is interested in saving money. What it is really doing is doubling the load borne by those who have been carrying the load all along, the employees and their employers, while not doing anything to ensure that the UIC cheats are shut off from the program.
The new legislation will double the waiting period applicable to those who quit their jobs, making it six weeks instead of three. This might discourage some of the abuses, but there must be more careful scrutiny of those who quit their jobs and more strenuous efforts to screen out those who do so simply to draw UIC benefits.
I repeat, the program must be made to serve the interests and welfare of those who support it with their premiums and who become employed through no fault of their own. Also, it must be administered in such a way as to screen out those who are professional UIC cheats. One way of doing this would be to lengthen the period of insured employment required as qualification for benefit. Right now, a person can work for eight weeks, get fired deliberately and then draw benefits for about half a year.

No act or program should rely on a huge bureaucracy for its reasonable application and proper implementation. Nor should it depend upon a Big Brother system of reporting indiscretions. No unemployment insurance program that I would like to see would depend upon an employer, a friend, even a relative, bringing indiscretions of people defrauding the act to the attention of the authorities. I think the incentive to remove oneself from the unemployment insurance rolls should be implicit in the program itself.
With this in mind, I have on several occasions made a proposal to the minister and I make it once more for his consideration and the consideration of his officials. I refer to the proposition of diminishing returns. Let a person receive full benefits for a period, say, of three to four weeks. Following that period, if benefits were reduced by 20 or 25 per cent, and then after another two weeks by 10 or 15 per cent, I think we would find that no one would stay on unemployment insurance for 40 or 50 weeks. Reduced benefits would soon put them into the labour market, which is where they should be.

Since we limit the premiums under the act and the level of salaries on the basis of which the payment of premiums is made, I think it would be just as acceptable to limit yearly earnings. I think we must place a maximum on the earnings one can have and continue to receive unemployment insurance. It would be better, as a general principle, to distribute a universal guaranteed income than to have thousands of people taking advantage of their tax paying neighbours and Canadian citizens.

We all know of the terrible abuses that take place under this act. I am sure most of us have been personally involved with individuals who complain about their neighbours and friends in this regard. Employers are often accomplices in this fraud. How many employers use the unemployment insurance system as a means of staff planning? How many employers let their people go in the wintertime with an agreement that they will collect unemployment insurance for a certain period of time and be compensated for the balance when they return to work? These are the same employers who criticize and complain to me about the overgenerous benefits of our system. They suggest we should cut half these people off benefits. Let me remind these employers that they can start at home by cutting the people they do not want receiving unemployment insurance benefits, and by making sure they do not have this type of agreement which is favourable to some employees and unfavourable to others.
How many employees who are receiving unemployment insurance have full-time jobs? I suggest there are many of them. Not only are they illegally receiving unemployment insurance benefits, but they do not pay tax on the added income they get from the full-time or part-time job. With that sort of activity becoming acceptable, I say we are creating a very bad social system and a very bad attitude among the population.
While it is true that there are many abuses by claimants, it is also true that there are many abuses to those claimants carried out by officers of the unemployment insurance service. This works both ways. I am under the impression, and I think there is some validity to this, that promotions in many instances are given in the unemployment insurance department on the basis of the number of convictions or disentitlements an officer has under his belt or can effect, rather than on the basis of the service he can provide the claimant or unemployed individual who seeks his service. This is something that should be looked into by the minister and changed.
I have made representations to the minister regarding abuses by officers. The one that has bothered me most relates to statements by claimants. I am pleased to see that the minister in his wisdom has decided to change that regulation, making sure that such a statement does not become a statement of evidence on the part of the claimant. These statements can be misinterpreted by an officer. I remember the case of one chap who was asked how much money he would like to earn in a new job if one was found for him. He said: "Well, I have a family of six kids and I can hardly support them under $100 a week". The officer put down on the statement, "Will not accept under $100 a week", disentitling the claimant immediately.
That is the type of thing I want to see stopped. I think it is the type of thing that will be stopped under the new procedure of obtaining a report from the officer, rather than a signed statement by the claimant. It seems to me the board of referees will be much better served by having both sides of the story before making a decision on the appeal, rather than just the side given by the officer as
Adjournment Motion
well as, perhaps, a misinterpreted but signed statement by the claimant.
I completely agree with the amendment in the bill that doubles the period for people who leave work without just cause or, indeed, refuse suitable employment. With regard to the 65 years of age clause, I know it is difficult to take away from people something you have given them and to which they have grown accustomed. However, I am sure our 65-year old people will understand the reasoning and thinking of the minister, his officials and the government as expressed in this clause. I simply cannot believe that a good insurance scheme can function when someone who pays $1,500 into the program can at a later date, when he reaches age 65, take $6,000 from the fund. This is economically impossible. I know our 65 year olds will understand this. You just cannot pay $1,500 in and some years later take out $6,000. If everybody did that, you would require four times the money to make the fund self-sustaining. So this part of the program is impossible to continue.
Let us remember the alternate benefits which accrue to those 65 years of age, including three weeks' unemployment insurance with no questions asked, old age security with no questions asked, the guaranteed income supplement-with an income test-and Canada Pension Plan benefits with no questions asked. We must also remember the additional income tax exemption of $1,307 for people over 65. While these alternate benefits may not completely supplant or replace unemployment insurance benefits, I think if people aged 65 will look at them closely they will see they are reasonable when compared to unemployment insurance.
I am in full agreement with the minister regarding the sickness provision. How many people have great difficulty in continuing to receive benefits as claimants when sick for a second time, even being sick for two or three days on the first occasion and seriously ill for an extended period the second time? I am in total agreement with, and commend the minister for, that particular change.
In conclusion, I hope the minister will continue to review the act. Personally, I am not satisfied that these changes will make it a perfect act, far from it, but I commend the minister for having had the courage at this time to bring forward the changes. I am convinced that he will find more beneficial amendments in the not too distant future.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would have a few remarks on this piece of legislation which is very important I think, and if I refer to the speeches I have just heard, it seems clearer and clearer that the minister will have to recognize some shortcomings in this bill and in the legislation on unemployment insurance as a whole. I understand hon. members on the government side who are very careful but, if you listened well to them, they try did to invite the minister to bring some corrections. I will refer later to the comments I heard.
Mr. Speaker, we have before us a piece of legislation which is important, I say it again, and which stems I think from an act which has been ill-administered for too long. I must say right away that I read carefully the speech made by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), who traced back the history of the legislation, and considering of course the credits being applied, it seems quite clear-and I did not hear anyone criticizing the allegations made by the hon. member for Hamilton West-that those previsions have always been wrong, which explains the loss of credibility towards the government only regarding this legislation. One could talk about so many other measures that have been put forward by the government for some time and which do not meet the needs and do not correct the situation.
Anyway, we are before a government which has been governing for ten years and we are once again before a legislation that is far from being popular and just. Yet, ten years ago, they were talking about a "just society". And most Canadians did believe it. Considering the inadequacy of that legislation, we feel increasingly that the public is losing confidence in a government that cannot manage to introduce acceptable measures which of course, we must criticize, exactly what we are doing. There is talk of savings of $500 to $600 million through this legislation, of which the workers will have to assume half. The worker will have to pay 50 per cent, which will mean an increase of 30 per cent. Still, one bill tells us the increase must not exceed 10 per cent in the case of salaries. Some revel in fine words, while accepting that the worker's premium go up by 30 per cent: we feel that is unfair. Mr. Speaker, if the

government made the wrong forecasts, if it erred completely, that is no reason why the workers should pay the consequences.
This bill provides some worthy steps we will not question; for instance, we accept that the penalty be doubled for those who leave their jobs too easily; basically, we are not against that but, as one of my hon. colleagues pointed out, we feel that whoever left his job for what he considered just reasons, I suppose, and who appeals to the court, should not be the only one to appear before it: the employer should also be called upon to appear and prove that the report he made on the employee is acceptable to the court of appeal.
It is unfair and intolerable to pay benefits to workers who have once more quit their jobs for reasons the court will surely be interested to know. The employer ought to be compelled to give evidence to permit double checking, which is not at present provided for in the act.
The administration of riding offices was also questioned. I hasten to say-and to say it in the minister's presence- that the office in my riding can boast of a very competent director and highly-qualified staff. However, in spite of the greatest efforts and the best of intentions, it does happen that some applicants encounter difficulties. For example, becausee the claim procedure is initiated in my riding office, the cheque must be made outside. Right now, as is so often the case, postal workers are on strike, which results in applicants experiencing a great deal of problems. Therefore I would like to urge the minister to provide ways and means whereby applicants can receive their cheques without delay. It is precisely the one who cannot afford to wait for his pay cheque that most needs the unemployment insurance benefits. Is it possible to improve this system to prevent claimants, once their form is duly completed and their acceptance acknowledged, having to wait 24 hours to get their cheque? All members hope to see this mechanism sufficiently well organized in order that justice be done to claimants in such circumstances.
Mr. Speaker, some provisions of this legislation are valuable. We regret and criticize the general administration and the estimates made some ten years ago, particularly because they were wrong or badly prepared.
A while ago I noted the member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Joyal) clearly requesting the minister not to deprive persons of 65 and willing to go on working from the possibility of drawing unemployment insurance benefits.
And at this point, Mr. Speaker, we of the opposition, and the New Democratic Party as well as the Social Credit Party of Canada, made suggestions, representations to the minister about that particular clause. We believe that those people want to remain in the labour force. And God knows, Mr. Speaker, since the government made its intentions known a few months back already-and I am convinced that other members think as I do-that representations have been made by the people concerned who want to remain in the labour force and qualify for unemployment insurance benefits. And the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont is one of the few members of the party in power to express his views clearly. That is a good thing and I congratulate him for it. The opposition did not wait until today to do that.
November 3, 1975

Since that legislation was introduced in the House, we have asked the minister to review that proposal, and I dare hope other members will do the same. The hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Roy) made a few very appropriate remarks on the administration in general, and I think it is important that members, whatever party they represent, tell the minister that there is a shortcoming and a proposal that is unacceptable.
So, in the circumstances, I hasten, Mr. Speaker, to urge the minister to lend an attentive ear about that particular clause. I feel it is my duty to ask the minister on behalf of those people to reconsider his decision and allow those who still want to remain in the labour force to qualify once again for unemployment insurance benefits. Of course, we must try today to amend a piece of legislation that was passed more than 30 years ago and also underwent certain amendments. I might ask why once again we have to deal with estimates amounting to millions, billions rather, why we have to find that kind of money and collect more from the worker in the present increasingly difficult situation.
As I said, in the unemployment area, there has been an attempt in the last ten years to mislead members of the House as well as the Canadian people in general with measures designed to reduce unemployment. I must remind this House, for the tenth time I believe, that unemployment rose from the 175,000 figure in 1968 to the current 600,000 or 700,000 level. I believe there is an attempt to have us live with a high unemployment rate, but we do not accept that.
As opposition members, we have a duty to ask for much more significant measures than those proposed until now. Not so long ago, not more than a year and a half ago, we were told that action was being taken to slow down inflation and reduce unemployment at the same time. Those were formal commitments. A vote of confidence was obtained from a majority of Canadians, but, as has not been realized for a few months in the face of this government's about-face in any areas, its credibility is jeopardized.
There are still shortcomings in this legislation. It is totally unfair to the worker and it is not only our right but our duty to urge this government to listen to reason and come forward with measures that are much more practicable and fair, and more in keeping with the just society that was sold to us ten years ago but did not materialize.
I urge the minister to show real understanding and much more compassion for the workers, the people that want to remain in the labour force and to qualify for the program by paying premiums. In this way, the government will not only win the public's confidence, which is beside the point, but fill the pressing needs of those Canadians.
I refer again to the statement of the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont who said earlier that he feels that the people are concerned and worried, that they are fed up with pieces of legislation inconsistent with their needs. In view of the lack of credibility of the government and the criticisms of the public and the opposition which are quite justified, he decided to ask the minister to reconsider his decision concerning the proposal, but why is he the only government member with enough courage to do so? It would be ridiculous to think, Mr. Speaker, that he is the only government member who had representations to
Unemployment Insurance Act
make in this regard. In my opinion, it is time to prove to the Canadian people that even if you are part of a team, you still have the sacred duty to bring the minister to reason when he is wrong. I feel it is important to stress this.
I therefore avail myself of this opportunity and of the invitation that he made to the minister to express my views. Of course, I could use the statements made earlier by my colleagues and the opinions expressed in the last few days, but I know that the government could reply: Of course, you are in the opposition and you have criticized, and that is all you can do.
We do not criticize because we like it, we ask for an amendment to a legislation which, I repeat, is obviously unfair to a certain group of Canadians. That is why we keep up this fight. We want to show the minister that we are right in hoping that others will take a stand as did the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont this afternoon. To my great surprise, this is the second time in a few days that the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont has made justified criticisms or serious recommendations to the government.
Last week, during the debate on price controls, he stated in the House that the ministers themselves fail to control the expenditures within their department. So, how can one imagine that it is possible to control prices and wages the ministers do not control expenditures within their own department? I am not the one who said so, it is a Liberal member. Today, he urged once again the minister to amend this clause in particular.
I insist on this clause, Mr. Speaker, as it is definitively the most harmful for those people and certainly the most unfair provision in this legislation. Of course, there are some amendment. We certainly wish that the administration will be better than ever and that claimant will get better services. There are more rigid measures, of course, and they are also justified, but we ask that this measure, this legislation be fairer than it is now. We should particularly eliminate this injustice where people aged 65 who wish to stay on the labour market are not entitled anymore to unemployment insurance benefits.
So Mr. Speaker, I repeat that it is unfair to try to recover those $250 million from the worker's pockets as it is unfair to deny those people the right to benefits. My comments will not be any longer but once more I encourage the members from government benches to show some guts and not only the members of the opposition but also a particular member. I saw some members that agreed before with the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont (Mr. Joyal) and I hope that we will show to the minister that we do not agree with this measure in its totality and that if this legislation is not amended at the committee stage to bill the loopholes we can foresee, these hon. members will also have the courage to vote against a piece of legislation that is unfair for a particular class of people.
I hope that the minister will take note of all the remarks made from this side of the House and that there will be similar comments to bring the minister to his senses so that Parliament will give Canadians a legislation that really meets the needs of workers and Canadian people.

Unemployment Insurance Act

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that this afternoon we are being treated, as we are on many days, to a parading of all the injustices and abuses that are going on in the UIC. My colleague, the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Roy), mentioned earlier that often people collect unemployment insurance for a period of 51 weeks. I would remind him, and members of the opposition, that the average person draws unemployment insurance for only 16 weeks and very few indeed collect from the full period. I would refer specifically to the provision in the bill lowering to 65 the age at which unemployment insurance coverage ceases.

The decision to lower the maximum age to get unemployment insurance coverage under the Unemployment Insurance Act stems from a number of fundamentals. One of them is the very nature of the plan. The Unemployment Insurance Act provides a protection against income losses in various circumstances and for a certain amount of time. It is not a retirement fund, but a temporary insurance against possible salary losses. When protection ends, premiums are in no way refundable. Fron that point of view, unemployment insurance is similar to a fire protection policy. If a fire breaks out, compensation is paid, but if there is no fire and the house is sold or torn down, fire insurance premiums are not refunded to the policyholder.
Anyway, there is no direct financial relationship between the cost of premiums and the amount of income protection under the plan. For instance, a person who would have been working since the plan was introduced in 1941 and always had the maximum insurable earnings would have contributed a total of $1,500 to the plan in September 1975. If this person came to lose his or her employment because of compulsory retirement at 65 and submitted a claim, he or she would be entitled to $6,373 over the maximum period of 51 weeks during which benefits a payable, provided the national and regional employment rates are high and he or she cannot secure employment.
A three-week retirement benefit is payable to major attachment claimants when they reach age 65, and this will remain under Bill C-69. The benefit is an acknowledgment of the reduced protection available to workers in the final year before their sixty-fifth birthday. Third, the principle of coverage being extended only for the normal working life of the claimant was recognized in the 1971 act when coverage was terminated at age 70. Labour groups, members of parliament and the general public have long advocated that most forms of social security for senior citizens begin at age 65, or even earlier in some cases, in recognition of the fact that the average working person has the right and the need to retire at that age and that other forms of income support should be available to him.
The Canada Pension Plan particularly has been upgraded. The earnings test has been eliminated and the plan itself reaches full maturity in 1976. These were concerns expressed by members of parliament in 1970 and 1971 when the Unemployment Insurance Act was being debated. They 
felt that the Canada Pension Plan did not provide adequate income replacement because at that time it had not reached full maturity and was earnings-tested. Other programs have also been improved. For example, in 1971 the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec Pension Plan afforded recipients $65. In 1975 we see that this has risen to $130. The old age security was $80 in 1971 and today it is $126.
