Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the government is meeting its moral obligations with regard to people 65 years of age and over. Hon. members will note that all these programs have been indexed. In addition, a $500 increase in the personal income tax exemption for persons aged 65 to 70 was made in 1972, bringing the total personal exemption for this age group to $1,000 more than for other taxpayers. This exemption has also been indexed.
The government operates its programs on limited financial resources, and time and time again we hear members of the opposition saying, "Cut back here" and "Cut back there."

speechtext: For whom?

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
For those who are unemployed, that is for whom. In terms of unemployment insurance, that need is clearly in the provision of employment income protection for people who are still in the normal working period of their lives. After retirement age has been reached, other programs take over to offer income support.

Apparently a number of people from this age group are using the unemployment insurance plan for purposes other than those for which it was intended. For instance, recent inquiries by Statistics Canada on labour market have consistently established that fewer persons declare being unemployed for the inquiry purposes than the actual number of claimants. That seems to indicate that those persons say to the inquirers that they are not looking for a job or not interested in finding one while they get unemployment benefits and report to the UIC that they actively look for a job. So it is increasingly difficult, from an administrative point of view, to ascertain whether the unemployed 65 or more are actually willing to work.
November 3, 1975

We must also recognize that people in that age group have difficulties finding a job. It is not always easy to look for a job when there are much younger prospects who report daily-these days anyway. The usual requirements for actively seeking employment with which all claimants must comply are excessively difficult for elderly workers who have serious employment problems. As the commission must apply the same requirements to all claimants, people of 65 or more do experience significant problems. [English]
I submit that this amendment will be understood. I suggest that it will be accepted by people 65 years of age and over.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to confine most of my remarks to clause 34 of Bill C-69, the clause dealing with social insurance numbers and the issuing of cards. However, I wish to say a few words about abuses generally with regard to unemployment insurance. Whenever someone on this side talks about tightening up unemployment insurance regulations to catch violators, someone opposite always mentions the high level of unemployment in some part of Canada and suggests that we are trying to disallow some unfortunate persons. This is not really the case and that is certainly not our purpose. But there are people who work the system, so to speak, and who have found the key to enable them to milk the fund for all they can get. Those are the ones we are talking about.
For instance, we are aware of certain large retailers who use the Unemployment Insurance Act to their advantage. What they do is quite legal, but in my view it is not very moral. They have a stable of workers whom they hire for short periods of time, lay them off and take on other workers for a short period of time. Then when the clerks are laid off, they apply for unemployment insurance. After a few weeks on unemployment insurance, they will be rehired, continue working for a period of time and then they are laid off again. The benefit to the employer is that these people are temporary or probationary workers, and as such they are not eligible for any of the normal fringe benefits given to regular employees. There is a turnover of thousands of people during the course of a year. The Unemployment Insurance Commission finances this stable of people with benefits. I cannot suggest any way to stop this, but it is happening now and did not happen before. It happens now with more and more companies and it is one of the abuses which somewhere along the line must be dealt with.
The other problem I see in my part of the country has to do with farm labour. A few years ago the available farm labour gathered on the outskirts of the city of Hamilton at Dundurn Castle. The local market gardeners would arrive at 6 a.m. and pick up their fieldhands for the day, delivering them back after the day's work to the same place. Some bright clerk in the Unemployment Insurance Commission office in Hamilton read the fine print in the regulations which said that if a person is employed more than 25 days per year, unemployment insurance premiums must be deducted. This bright lad created havoc in the market garden industry. People used to work for the summer at the market gardens and never worried about unemployment insurance or income tax because they did not earn
Unemployment Insurance Act
enough to bother the income tax department: most earned less than $1,000.
What happened to these people? They now pay unemployment insurance premiums, their employers have to pay their portion as well and they must keep records of earnings and deductions. These people would rarely seek unemployment insurance benefits when the market gardening season was over. Many people took it as a part-time job during the summer. They went back to school, or many who were housewives went back to their normal home duties in the fall when the children went back to school. Some of them worked during the summer on farms to earn enough money to take a winter holiday. I suggest that this was the situation in most parts of the country where there was market gardening.
Now we have to import field hands from Mexico and the Caribbean to fill the void, at considerable cost to this country's taxpayers. I might add that the calibre of work done by these imported field hands is high. The farmers like them and want them back. I mention this as an example of government interference with the private sector. It is working to the detriment of market gardens and adding to the cost of the unemployment insurance program.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Do not forget the tobacco farmers.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I ought not to forget the tobacco farmers. They are important.
I turn now to clause 34 dealing with social insurance numbers and cards issued by central records. I feel somewhat responsible for this particular mendment to the act and commend the minister for bringing it in. We often talked about it when we met in the halls before the bill was introduced. He assured me that the amendment would be included and I commend him for it. He is a man of his word and I admire him greatly.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: It is just that it takes him a long time to act.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Leverage is something members of parliament learn to use, to move the bureaucracy of government from its rigid and inflexible position. One must learn where to put the lever and how much pressure to apply in order to obtain the desired movement. It is an art you must learn by experience. You begin from the position that the government thinks it never does anything wrong and that those at the top, the senior bureaucrats, in their wisdom believe they know what is best for the people. Given that fact, you find difficulty in placing the levers in the proper position. But if you persevere, you can win.
Early in March, 1974, a young man named Gary Hapke, from Dundas, near my home town, came to my home one Sunday with a problem. He told me an amazing story, of having had his pocket picked at a circus in 1970 and of someone, unknown to him, using his identity. He explained that he had to justify his income tax claim each year to the officials of the Department of National Revenue because his impersonator was ' accepting employment in Mr. Hapke's name and under his social insurance number.

November 3, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
Further, the impersonator used Mr. Hapke's driver's licence and, during a series of months, had collected several traffic violations, fraud charges, and a conviction for stealing a car, all in Gary Hapke's name. Here was this young man trapped between three layers of government.
Through the efforts of Hon. George Kerr, then solicitor general of Ontario, we arranged to erase the traffic violations, the stolen car charge and fraud charges standing in his name on provincial records. Frankly, I did not know where to begin. Mr. Hapke and I talked to the local police, and met with Staff Sergeant Smith of the Regional Police of the Hamilton area. He was extremely helpful in the initial stages of the matter, and provided background detail which showed the immensity of the fraudulent impersonation which had been taking place. The problem was that it was difficult to move the bureaucracy in Ottawa and get them to clear Mr. Hapke's name in their records. I had already taken the position that a new social insurance number should be issued to Mr. Hapke so that he could go on his way; then, if more charges arose, the income tax people could know that they were attributable to the impersonator and not to Mr. Hapke. In the meantime Mr. Hapke's name and social insurance number kept turning up all over the country, even as far west as British Columbia.
I wrote detailed letters to four cabinet ministers, the then minister of national revenue, the then minister of justice, the Minister for Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras), and the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand), in an attempt to straighten out this matter. It was necessary to get those four cabinet ministers to act.
It was necessary for the Department of National Revenue to clear the income tax files so that Mr. Hapke could get a tax refund to which be was entitled by virtue of tax overcharge.
The Solicitor General and the RCMP had to act, to apprehend the impersonator. We knew his name and the RCMP, as it turned out, had his fingerprints on file.
The Minister of Manpower and Immigration had to act, to clear the UIC files covering Mr. Hapke's name, and to issue a new social insurance number from central records.
The then minister of justice had to act to charge the impersonator, once apprehended, with impersonation and fraudulent use of government documents.
By a stroke of luck we learned, through Inspector Sam Eyre of the Hamilton-Wentworth Regional Police, that the person using Gary Hapke's name was one Roger Sasser-ville, then serving a sentence in Oxford county jail for fraud. I immediately rose in the House and asked the Solicitor General if he would now proceed with charges against Mr. Sasserville for impersonating Mr. Hapke, using his social insurance number, and so on. To my surprise the Solicitor General replied that he did not know whether the matter fell within his jurisdiction. I received the same replies from the then minister^ of justice and the then minister of national revenue. I only received satisfaction from the Minister of Manpower and Immigration, who said he would look into it.
At about this time I got in touch with the head of the central records branch of the Department of Manpower and Immigration to see what could be done about issuing

Mr. Hapke a new social insurance number. To my surprise he told me that this could only be done if Mr. Hapke would change his legal name. I questioned this gentleman several times. He told me he had cleared the matter with the legal officers of the department and that this was the only way a new social insurance number could be issued. I was also told that the computer was not programmed to handle two numbers in connection with the same name. This was nonsense, as I was soon to learn.
As a result of the publicity given this matter several people wrote to me. I heard from an employer in Toronto who had several employees who possessed two, three and, in one case, four social insurance cards. He told me that he had recorded their social insurance numbers on their T-4 slips. I do not know whether the Department of National Revenue has looked into this matter. The danger of that situation is that a man might be employed under one number and collect unemployment insurance under another. In one case this could be duplicated three or four times. The situation, of course, was ridiculous. Here was a young man whose name had been used fraudulently, who had a record on RCMP files not of his own making, who had been harassed for four years by National Revenue for non-payment of taxes on income he had not earned, and whose personal credit record was filled with charges that were not of his making. He was now being asked to change his name legally in order to secure a new social insurance number. It was said that this was necessary in order to straighten out the record.
He was probably the most depressed young man I have run into for years. When he came to me he had applied for a job with a computer company, he having studied computer science at the university. When the firm checked his record with a credit reporting agency it found three or four charges standing against his name. There was a charge for car theft, numerous traffic violations, and other charges that did not relate to him at all. After we brought this matter into the open events began to move more rapidly.
I happened to find out that the man who was impersonating my constituent was in jail in Woodstock in Oxford County. One Sunday I visited him for two hours. He told me a most amazing story of how he travelled across Canada and the United States using the identity of another man. While there, I examined the visitors' book back to the time that this man Sasserville was admitted to jail. I found that no one from any government agency had visited or interviewed him with regard to the fraudulent use of government records and Mr. Hapke's name.
I did this because, after there had been several critical newspaper articles about this matter, someone wrote to the editor of the Globe and Mail over the signature of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras). The letter stated that the commission had traced this person
November 3, 1975

and was taking action. I know the minister did not write the letter. The person who did write it knew that this was an outright lie because the commission had not or was not taking any action. That is why I searched through the visitors' book to see who had been there since the man had been admitted. I talked with prison officials as well.
I know the minister did not write the letter. One of his executive assistants wrote it. Every day we see ministers in here with three or four books filled with letters requiring signatures. The minister is a busy man. He probably signed the letter without reading it. Had he read it, I am sure he would not have signed it.
I read the letter in the Globe and Mail. I replied to the editor and straightened out the record. It seemed odd that a minister of the Crown would correspond with a member of parliament through letters to the editor in a newspaper.
We then had some action on this matter. The then Minister of National Revenue responded by refunding the taxes paid. I sincerely thank him for that. He was the first to take any real action. They then refunded the taxes paid by Mr. Hapke on funds earned by Mr. Sasserville. All the traffic violations were cancelled and a new driver's licence was issued to Mr. Hapke.
The money paid for traffic fines was refunded and the fraud charges in Ontario standing in Mr. Hapke's name were cancelled. In fact only two things remained to be cleared. We had to have his record on file with the RCMP expunged, and a new social insurance number issued.
After considerable difficulty we had Mr. Hapke's records expunged by the RCMP. I say difficulty. That is really an understatement. I watched the Solicitor General (Mr. All-mand) over television one evening. He was telling a reporter that he was endeavouring to have criminal records cleared when a criminal has had no charge for five years. Here we were with a man who had not committed a crime and we could not get his record cleared.
A strange thing happened. The Solicitor General actually sent me a fingerprint card and asked me to fingerprint my constituent, Mr. Hapke. Can you imagine a minister of the Crown asking a member of parliament to fingerprint a constituent who had committed no crime? It was a ludicrous situation. I said the man had not committed a crime, so why should I have him fingerprinted. I said to the minister that he had charges standing in this name and an RCMP detachment in Hamilton. If he was that concerned about it, why did he not have this man arrested. The minister would not do that. I could not understand why the RCMP did not investigate the matter.
After persistent prodding of the various ministers, they finally moved to charge Mr. Sasserville with fraudulent use of government records and Mr. Hapke's name. And after this was completed, we finally had Mr. Hapke's record cleared by the RCMP. Through the RCMP, and I give them credit for this, we got Mr. Hapke's original wallet and records returned.
This chap Sasserville had gone to the United States. He became involved with the Texas state police and the FBI. They deported him to Canada. They removed his wallet and, by God, there was Mr. Hapke's social insurance card, driver's licence, and birth certificate.

I said it was concerned. I did not say it was a fact. Business is remembered as seeming socially impotent during the dark days of the depression. This was one of the main stimuli to growth in the size and power of governments and unions. The out-of-work experience is

not only impoverishing but degrading for the honest worker.
Our unemployment insurance plan is not only a permanent feature of our way of life but is recognized by other countries, including the U.S.A., as being one of the best. Nevertheless it warrants continuous review and occasional amendment as times change.
That is exactly what Bill C-69 is all about. These amendments attempt to improve the plan, mainly by doing three things. First, a larger proportion of the premium payments will be paid by the employer and employee, and less by the government, which is being urged on all sides to reduce its spending. Second, it tightens up some areas of the plan in order to discourage abuse. Third, it further rationalizes the plan by eliminating benefits in a social area already covered-I refer in this case to retired people who already receive pensions or who may prefer to continue working.
Such cost saving measures, which also help tidy up and tighten the plan, deserve the support of all Canadians, including those who criticize the government. Unfortunately this is expecting too much from the other side. Responsible action by the government has been greeted only by partisan political bickering. Undoubtedly further changes and improvements will be made from time to time. This bill was not designed to be all-inclusive and final.
On the other hand, in all honesty it must be acknowledged that there is broadly based concern shared by the public over several aspects of the program as it now stands. Some of these concerns involve the terms of the law, some the way in which it is administered, and most reflect a general social malaise related to the economy.
Real abuses probably do occur, in spite of the best efforts of the UIC office workers. Some can and should be corrected, some are very difficult to cope with in practice. In my own unemployment insurance district there are about 12,000 claims on the books at any one time. Of these about 10 per cent are subject to special investigation, and of that number about 70 per cent are rejected as not being valid. This represents a great deal of work and a high level of responsibility.
One might suggest to the public that they report cases of abuse which come to their attention, but people do not appear to relish such a responsibility. Some critics insist that applicants should have to take any kind of job, in any part of the country. It could also become very anti-democratic for our society.
Last year the standard stereotype for the abuser of the plan was the young, long haired, anti-social hippie dropout. This year the spotlight has shifted to the middle aged, more respectable types who have on and off concepts of work, housewives and other women, seasonal workers, students of all ages, and so on. Paying into the unemployment insurance fund is just an added task they must accept every day and every month they work. Now the government says it wants more of their money. The government tells the people they must pay more for working every day. There must be a method whereby these people when they reach age 65 are not cut off and cut out.
We should have a scheme whereby those who work and never draw benefits but pay into the fund day in and day out would be able to receive some benefit in a realistic way at the end of their working careers. When it comes to unemployment and unemployment insurance, the Conservatives now take second prize. The Liberals have made unemployment slightly worse than we had in 1959, 1960 and 1961, if anybody would care to check the figures. In fact the hon. member made the same mistake as the Liberal spokesmen have been doing since 1968, referring to an increase in employment but neglecting to mention the increase in unemployment when the Conservatives were in power from 1958 to 1962. I should like to remind the House that in 1926 an hon. member of this place secured a letter from the then Prime Minister of Canada containing a commitment for old age pensions immediately, and sympathetic consideration for a system of unemployment insurance. This did not in fact happen until the period of 1940-41. It only took another 13 or 14 years to get that from the Liberal government. However, I can also recall as a kid in the dirty thirties hearing the Tories say that if there were an unemployment insurance plan it would destroy the incentive to work, and there would be abuses with people stealing public funds and defrauding the public. In fact we heard Tories in those days talk about stopping old age pensions because they would destroy the incentive to work. I find it amusing now that in dealing with this legislation these great friends of the working people are associating working men with businessmen.
I should like to remind my hon. friends on both the government and official opposition sides that in spite of all their propaganda, talk, innuendo, inference, and blame about so-called abuses and misuse of unemployment insurance, the reason for the fantastic deficits in the unemployment insurance fund and for the expenditures required at the expense of taxpayers is not because the claimants and beneficiaries under UIC are lazy, no good, do not want to work, or want a free ride on the UIC fund; it is due to high unemployment and no other reason. sundry free enterprise spokesmen, columnists, and editorial writers that it is due to no-goods and free-riders who are abusing the unemployment insurance fund are untrue.
I was hoping for items in this legislation which would correct many of the problems every member of this House has had brought to his attention since the last time we dealt with a UIC bill, and I cannot find any. If each hon. member will check his correspondence for the last several years, there were literally hundreds and sometimes thousands of cases of UIC claimants who had been drawing benefits and then became disentitled, or were prevented from receiving benefits in the first place. I hope that some hon. members on the government side, including the minister, will consider the difficulties we have had, let alone claimants for UIC.
Let us talk about the matter of disentitlement. I see no improvements in this legislation which would correct the present act for the claimant who has been drawing benefits and is then called in for a job search interview and asked all those leading questions. He is not told what the ground rules and regulations are to begin with. Even if he is 100 per cent honest, he returns home and a week later receives a form letter, which may or may not have been signed, saying that he is disentitled.
The whole issue of what is suitable employment is reasonably well described in the legislation now, but it is badly applied. The matters of rates of pay which will be acceptable to the claimant and the commission, the kind of job the claimant can and will accept and is able to do, the limited area in which a claimant can or will work, are not covered in these amendments.
The minister is sitting here checking his mail, and I hope he has answered a few letters I have written to him in the last weeks, and will tell me what a member of parliament can say to a constituent who lives 87 miles from Regina who, when called in for a job search statement was asked many leading questions and then told that because she limited herself to employment in the village of Semans or within a radius of 25 miles, which included four or five other villages, she was disentitled because there were no employment opportunities in the villages of Semans, Govan, Strasbourg, Raymore and Nokomis. She was told that if she would seek employment in Regina and could prove that she was actively seeking employment 87 miles away, several times a week, they would reinstate her benefits.
I do not see anything in these amendments which will do anything about that kind of ridiculous situation. The policies of this government and its predecessors and large corporations denuded rural Canada of employment opportunities, did away with thousands of implement dealers, post offices, railway stations, oil company bulk stations, and other enterprises in rural Canada, which lost us tens of thousands of employment opportunities. However, if a person happens to live in a rural area and cannot find a job in the town or village in which he lives, and if he is not prepared to drive 75 or 100 miles two or three times a week-that is, each way-he is disentitled because he has limited himself to an area in which the commission says there are no opportunities for employment. The government's legislation is not designed to treat sensibly, decently, and in a civilized way people who lose jobs through no fault of their own, whether because of geography, climate, the kind of occupation they follow, or any other reason. It is not designed to help them.
The Tories have said little about this subject. With one breath, out of one side of their mouths, they talk about the poor working man; with the next breath, out of the other side of their mouths, they talk about abuses. I agree that a few people cheat on unemployment insurance. If they numbered as many as those who cheat in business, cheat on income tax or in corporate operations, our society would be in deep trouble. But the numbers are not large. Of course there are some abuses. Abuses are likely to arise in connection with any fund. The 1971 bill was designed to cut down abuses. Man's ingenuity in evading regulations is endless, especially in a society in which we teach our children, from the time they can stand, how to get around the law and regulations, and how to make a fast buck.

speechtext:
And ten of the 870 were sent to jail. That hardly qualifies as a massive abuse of the UIC fund. Why, this talk of abuse is nothing but lip, nothing but a crime perpetrated against an excellent social program. It is designed to do nothing less than give employers the chance to hire people, who would otherwise be unemployed, for cheap wages.
That brings me back to the whole business of the reasons for disentitlement, what one must do to be reinstated, and the rates of pay they will accept. Of course you can tell the fellow with the Bachelor of Arts, Bachelor of Education and teacher's certificate to sell shoes and dig ditches. But during his prior employment he may have purchased a home and have monthly payments of $200. In addition, he may have three or four children, and cannot support them by digging ditches or selling shoes.
What kind of a job will such a person accept? During the job search interview, he is asked leading questions. When it is put to him that he would not want to work for so much less than he earned before, quite naturally he says no, he would like to get $5 or $6 an hour as he was earning $8 an hour previously. If he is foolish enough to sign a statement saying he will not work for less than that amount, a week later he will receive a form letter, probably unsigned, saying that he is disentitled because he limited himself to the amount of pay for which he will work.
There is a stacked deck against those who are normally hard-working, who have contributed to the fund, and who are unemployed when there are high rates of unemployment. The deficit which the government faced in the last several years in the UIC fund is not because of abuses but because of high unemployment. Surely the government could have learned a lesson from its fight against inflation in 1969 and 1970 when unemployment rates jumped almost in direct proportion to its fight against inflation, something ministers claimed they had wrestled to the ground.
The government now proposes a new battle against inflation without at the same time fighting unemployment. It brings in legislation that nit-picks around the edges and that does not provide a fair shake or fair hearing for those claiming unemployment insurance benefits, legitimately or not.
It is even difficult to defraud the UIC fund, something for which we should be grateful. In fact four years ago, the government and parliament devised legislation that was pretty good. It is the application of that legislation with which members on all sides quarrel. We quarrel with how it is interpreted and applied.
When the minister returns to his office I invite him to read the correspondence I have been quoting. I refer him to an application for leave to appeal dated September 17 which was rejected by the chairman. If he will check further he will see correspondence to which, to my knowledge, he has not replied. I quote the correspondence:

November 3, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
-the procedure outlined under the Unemployment Insurance Act is highly improper. When it is felt that the Board of Referees have widely mis-construed the purpose of the act, the materials before the board, previous decisions of the Unemployment Insurance Commission, the wording of the statute, the proper remedy is to appeal. If this amounts to a recapitulation-I do not feel that this is a proper grounds for denying an appeal. Furthermore, the chairman of the board of referees in the case in question was in fact the party who put forth their interpretation of Section 40(2) of the act. To ask him to allow an appeal on the basis of his interpretation is asking a lot of a human being.
It is asking a lot, even if he were impartial.
It is suggested that his interpretation is in fact faulty and that with this in mind it would only be proper to submit the case to a higher authority for clarification as to the correct interpretation of the section.
Section 40(2) deals with suitable employment. I wish the minister would read it and make his officials apply it. Section 40(2) reads:
40(2) For the purposes of this section but subject to subsection (3) employment is not suitable employment for a claimant if it is:
(b)	Employment in his usual occupation either at a lower rate of earnings or on conditions less favourable than those observed by agreement between employers or employees, or in the absence of any such agreement, than those recognized by good employers;
I suppose we in this House should say that most employers are good employers.
(c)	Employment of the kind other than employment in his usual occupation either at a lower rate of earnings or on conditions less favourable than those conditions that he might reasonably expect to obtain,-
Mark the next words:
-having regard to those conditions that he habitually obtained in his usual occupation, or would have obtained had he continued to be so employed.
That is the way the act reads at the moment. This person with the Bachelor of Arts, Bachelor of Education and teacher's certificate was told by the board of referees that he could sell shoes or dig ditches. I cite this only as an example of thousands of cases of people denied appeals by the chairmen of the boards of referees who ruled them out of court in the first place. This is not justice of any kind, including poetic. There is nothing in this legislation to correct that kind of situation.
I am not worried about abuses of the unemployment insurance fund. Whatever percentage of abuses there may have been in the worst period of time over the last number of years is minuscule compared to the thousands and thousands of people in this country who began to draw benefits and were later disentitled for a variety of reasons. They may have refused to drive 200 miles to work. They may have a university degree and not be fussy about digging ditches. By limiting themselves to the kind of occupation they will accept, they are disentitled.
It is very natural to limit one's self to an occupation. If a person knows only one or two kinds of jobs, he may be careful about signing a paper to the effect that he will accept several kinds of employment. I would hesitate to volunteer to a UIC search officer that I am willing to do a job that I know nothing about and in which I have no experience. I could lie, accept the job, last two days and then be fired. The commission would then say that, according to the act, I have been fired for just cause and, therefore, am not entitled to benefits. The deck is stacked against anyone who is work conscientious. It is stacked

against him under the present legislation, and even more so with these amendments.
If the government had brought in with its so-called improvements to the legislation some kind of program for full employment, in co-ordination and conjunction with its program to fight inflation, it would have some sympathy in this House. However, as it is now proposing to amend the act, there is no way that I or many other members can support it. The government must be prepared to come up with a lot more. It must recognize instances such as those I have cited. Cases have also been cited by the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling), and others.
Until the government is prepared to do more, it should not be surprised that we oppose its amendments. It should not be surprised that some of us at least are not prepared to co-operate with its so-called phoney fight against inflation. We also object to its measures when it fails to bring in a program of full employment.
The mess in the government's housing program was compounded today by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Danson). We are now confronted with these bad amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act, an act which could otherwise be made to work in a fair, equitable, and just manner. It is adequate to eliminate, rule out, or catch up with those who abuse or misuse the UIC fund. The minuscule number who do that should be thoughtless of and more thought should be given to the hundreds of thousands who are denied benefits or have them cut off, people who are not lazy no-goods, but people who want to work.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Order, please. I regret I must interrupt the hon. member, but his time has now expired.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Bill C-69, concerning unemployment insurance and still under discussion in the House today, has more specifically the following objective indicated in the bill itself and I quote:
An Act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971 to add, in the manner provided, a new class to the existing classes of insurable employment; to provide, in the manner prescribed, for changes in qualifying periods, benefit periods, entitlement to benefits and, rates of benefits; to provide, in the manner prescribed, for a new basis for the calculation that determines the proportion of the basic cost of benefit for a year that will be borne by the Government; to make the employer's premiums of Her Majesty in right of Canada payable by statute; and to provide for the payment of allowances to persons or their representatives who attend before an umpire on an appeal from a decision of the Minister.
All these fine words, Madam Speaker, merely to say that the government has decided to go into action and apply the axe to the existing Unemployment Insurance Act in an attempt to save Canada from the claws of inflation. If we wanted to introduce this bill in more simple and more concrete terms, one could simply say, at the beginning of the text, the following:
His Excellency the Governor General has recommended to the House of Commons the present measure to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1971, in such manner as to allow the federal government to ride roughshod over the unemployed who are mostly responsible for the economic problems facing our country. This image may appear a
November 3, 1975

little exaggerated, but nobody can sincerely say that it is not to a great extent realistic. What strikes me most and prompts me to make such a comparison is the fact that Bill C-69 is the very first important bill to be discussed in this House immediately after the Anti-inflation Act.
Yet the first people the government is tackling, supposedly to curb its expenses, are those very people who are already in trouble on the social and economic levels-the unemployed-as if those people were the first responsible for the inflationary crisis facing this country. If we want to be in the least honest, 1 ef us admit that unfortunately those people are rather among the victims who have to get along as well as they can in a situation where jobs are growing scarce. Besides I honestly feel, and all hon. members in the House will agree with me, that the unemployed who actually do not want to work account only for a very small minority and that the vast majority of the unemployed would be very glad to get overnight a decent job to provide for their families and lead a normal life.
Madam Speaker, being close to those people, listening to their problems, as the true role of a member of parliament requires, is enough to realize that most unemployed did not choose their situation. Quite the contrary, most of the time those people go through very trying, not to say in some cases tragic, experiences. I try as much as I can to keep in continuous and close contact with my constituents of Richmond riding and I know what is going on. I am sure that most members have heard of very sorry cases in their riding and that those people-I mean the unemployed-did not have much chance to express or defend themselves at the unemployment insurance office.
Officials, Madam Speaker, often keep back from the unemployed explanations on what the law contains and what they can do to get the chance of collecting a small amount of money every week to survive or pay their bills.
I want to blame directly the civil servants working in the unemployment insurance offices who never say anything to help the case of an unemployed worker progress, either by explaining to him or her what the situation of the file is, suggesting to him or her what avenues are available under the Unemployment Insurance Act, or simply telling him or her: "Sir, Madam or Miss, you must seek employment, and our conditions are such and such." No, they prefer to keep quiet and listen to the unemployed who is speaking and the next day, the situation is unchanged. The poor unemployed has only one privilege; to go and see his or her elected representative and say: Please help me; I have come to a dead-end and I cannot get my unemployment insurance benefits to which I think I am entitled.
In many cases, Madam Speaker, if only the officer at the unemployment insurance office, in Sherbrooke or somewhere else, had opened his mouth to explain to him-if he knew, of course-he probably does not know, he may not have read it. But if he knows, he should speak up and explain the problem to him, what bothers him, what stops him, what prevents him from receiving benefits, all that, the coming back and forth and sometimes the 70, 80 or 90 miles he must drive to go see his M. P. and say: Listen, you must help me, because I have problems with my unemployment insurance. All those things would not happen and we
Unemployment Insurance Act
would avoid those expenses, hardships and sacrifices of the unemployed in respect of their personal rights, if we had adopted a more humane legislation.
For all those reasons I find it inappropriate and even indecent to see the government, as its first anti-inflationary measure to cut those expenses, go after that class of citizens who are above all victims of the present economic situation, a measure which will only add to their problems, serious enough as they are.
Yesterday, Madam Speaker, I had the opportunity of reading the Senate Hansard for last Thursday, October 23. One speech held my attention in particular, that of Senator Perrault dealing with the economic situation and the current government offensive against inflation. It is worthy of note and it could, in particular, help us place Bill C-69 in its true context, and realize how nefarious its consequences could be.
The hon. senator indicated first of all that if inflation persists or increases, it can compromise an economic revival and merely increase unemployment; later on, he described the present situation with considerable eloquence and perception and I quote:
Of all evils that afflict our society, inflation is now without doubt the most intolerable and the most insidious. It is the most intolerable because, more than any other, it exacerbates social injustices by attacking first of all the weakest and the poorest of our citizens: those who live on fixed incomes. Those who see their life savings melt like butter in a saucepan. Finally, those who are not in a position to protect their purchasing power because they are in no way able to unite to defend their rights to an adequate income.
It is also the most insidious evil because we tend to consider inflation as a fatality against which we are helpless, except to save our own skin by sacrificing our neighbour's.
That last sentence, Madam Speaker, strikes me as unfortunately too true, and it could apply to Bill C-69 now before the House.
The government let problems pile up before reacting and now they are like a drowning man struggling desperately; they are trying to save their bacon by sacrificing their neighbour's. The worst off is the poor unemployed. The unemployed's bacon is sacrificed. They try to recover $1 billion at the poor's expense. How strange with a government which is supposedly democratic, which is reelected year after year. It looks like the electorate do not get fed up with being taken in. I say "taken in", Madam Speaker. In particular the poor are being "bought" for $2 often to vote or for something else. They are getting taken in again and again and they always vote the same way. Why? To be exploited. They cannot even afford any more to pay for their groceries.
Those of my colleagues on both sides of the House who refrain from speaking about this do so perhaps because they never went in a home where there are still children with bare feet in January, February and March. I do not exaggerate, Madam Speaker, I simply say the facts. When we go in the house, we hear: "I have been waiting for my unemployment insurance cheque for one month". In Montreal, the computers are out of order. I think that in several cases it is not the computers which are out of order but the brains of some administrators or some of our officers. That

November 3, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
is dangerous. A computer can be repaired, but brains very hardly.
Madam Speaker, what surprises me most in this bill is that the first scapegoat who falls under the hand of the governement is still the unemployed. Yet, in the same sense as indicated by the hon. senator, whom I cited earlier, they also are concerned and facing serious social injustices, because they are at a disadvantage in a sense, unable above all to protect their purchasing power which weakens day after day because of the rising cost of living. Before such clear and precise facts, this bill becomes still more illogical and even appears to come from another era, flying in the face of common sense as it does.
In fact, the bill was announced in the budget speech by the former minister of finance quite a while ago as he expressed his intention to cut down on government's expenses to break inflation. Even at that time, the bill would do not have been timely because it might have increased the uneasiness caused by inflation. It is just as simple as that. The poor are always blamed. It is very bold of a poor man to try to get $10 more than he is entitled to. But when a rich man manages through artful trickery to cheat the Department of National Revenue of $100,000 or even only $10,000, everyone in his accountant's office applauds, ulesss it is at the cocktail parties which are thrown here and there.
But not the poor. It is too bad, he just got $10, it is dangerous. He has nothing with which to defend himself and that is why he is abused. I think one could have at least expected this legislation to undergo in-depth changes to really help the unemployed, instead of crushing them, while putting in place at the same time the mechanisms necessary to avoid abuse and detect those who may take undue advantage of the unemployment insurance plan, something on which I agree entirely with the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras). By the way, I do not agree with creating generalized misery because of one-tenth of 1 per cent who take undue advantage of unemployement insurance.
Madam Speaker, I want to say that we of the Social Credit are going to vote against this bill because I think it does not lead anywhere and causes even more suffering in this country. If the bill is accepted, on the one hand, the government will save $560 million in benefits that it will no longer be paying out and, on the other hand, it will go out and get $490 million more in the form of employer-employee premiums which represents a considerable loss to people. The three-week period during which the unemployed are not entitled to benefits if they quit their jobs themselves will be increased to six weeks without serious consideration for reasonable human motives. Madam Speaker, this is very serious for the following reason: In certain parts of Canada, in the province of Quebec and in the Maritimes people work for $2.60 an hour to support a family of three, four or five children.
They are being forced under this new unemployment insurance legislation to wait six weeks before receiving their first cheque when they are already in the red because the basic salary does not provide a decent living for their families. They are being forced to wait six weeks on top of that, and they are being punished if they leave their jobs because they can no longer lfve on their salaries, let alone

provide a living for their families. Once again, I think it is scandalous in a rich country like ours.
Claimants with dependents will see their special benefits reduced from 75 per cent to 66% per cent while the cost of living increases steadily.
On the other hand, people aged 65 or more will not be entitled to benefits and will not contribute to the program any longer although they paid all their life without drawing benefits and this, under the pretext of reducing the overlapping of social security programs lest, I suppose, older people get too much security. Those are, Madam Speaker, some of the main provisions of this legislation that the government presents in a such positive way and that is supposed to help the unemployed and the government.
Who stands to gain help from that bill? Certainly not the unemployed, Madam Speaker. Some members of this House will say: This project will help the unemployed. And they add: We are going to recover $1 billion from the unemployed, the employers and the employees. Where is the logic, Madam Speaker? Where is the logic of those senior officials who are giving to this government such ideas that I consider unhuman and-well, I would rather not say the word.
I think now that you will better understand why I presented this legislation at the beginning of my speech. Anyway, even if the Liberal members might not admit it today, Canadians are ever more prepared to realize it at the next election. They are not the ones to blame, it is those who counsel them in the long term. And you step on to the beaten tracks to exploit the poor.
Besides, Madam Speaker, there is another point I insist on mentioning. The other day, when I listened to the speech of the minister, I was amazed to see how it is possible to sugar the pill, to disguise a situation, to even hide the truth, and seriously hope the people will still believe for some time that the Liberal moon is made of green cheese.
Indeed, when the government is cutting down benefits, increasing premiums, terminating unemployment coverage for persons aged 65 or over, and extending the waiting period in some instances, the minister introduces that very bill in the House, arguing that it is meant to contribute to the realization of one of the basic objectives of the social security study, and to do away with some of the unfairness and complications it gives rise to. Where are the complications the UIC gives rise to, when it increases from three to six weeks the waiting period for a person who leaves his employment because he is underpaid and life becomes impossible, for him, because his employer takes advantage of him, and so on. I could mention one thousand and one instances in my constituency, especially in footwear manufacturing and fashion businesses, where employees are trained from scratch.
They start training employees to make them profitable when they do piece work, because they are not profitable if they are paid a salary. They try to ruin them by having them do piece work and therefore be profitable. If the girl is not healthy enough to carry the burden, Madam Speaker, she has to leave. Well, they say, you can no longer do your
November 3, 1975

work because your health is not good, so you will be punished: No unemployment insurance benefits for six weeks, and after that you will go from door to door to try and get a job, and earn a living for your family. They think that is intelligent.
To me, it is about the same kind of logic as you can see in the papers respecting the recent visit of President Sadat in the United States. The Egyptian president wants to purchase American arms to maintain peace in the Middle East. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, Mr. Sadat and our Minister of Manpower and Immigration would get along very well since they seem to be on the same wavelength and seem to make the same kind of reasoning. One of them purchases arms to make peace-I am talking of Sadat, the intelligent Mr. Sadat-and the other strips the unemployed to give them social security and eliminate inequities. That is very intelligent!
With such a negative bill, the minister should immediately introduce compensation measures to balance forces though I very much doubt that he will do so. My Social Credit colleagues who spoke before me made several very valid proposals and even provided accurate figures and data in support of the these proposals. For my part, I would like to conclude by emphasizing two points which should be applied as soon as possible to support the economy and the labour market.
First of all, the government should immediately establish a special program to systematically create productive employment. For instance, instead of providing $150 million for LIP projects which last only six months, it should allocate half of this to social welfare and to support all types of poor people with productive employment projects.
Such action would reasonably stimulate the economy while lowering the unemployment rate, which would reduce proportionately the difficulties of the Unemployment Insurance Commission and allow the maintenance of normal benefits and certain facilities.
On the other hand, it is more than time to establish a true guaranteed minimum income system which would support the poorest or those who have temporary employment problems and, at the same time, progressively reduce to a certain extent the responsibilities of the Unemployment Insurance Commission. In my opinion, they have their hands full. They cannot even advise the unemployed about the law.
I think that this method is much more practical that that proposed in the bill we are now discussing. In practice, Bill C-69 increases the number of bureaucrats, worsens the complexities already existing in the present legislation, cuts or lowers benefits to claimants and raises premiums.
In conclusion, one can say that this legislation does not benefit anybody, except the government which considers Bill C-69 a governmental self-financing mechanism operated by the unemployed.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for the opportunity to say a few words on the important subject of unemployment insurance and the amendments proposed in Bill C-69.
Unemployment Insurance Act
For three years the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) has resisted attempts, both within parliament and outside parliament, to weaken the rights of the unemployed in Canada. In my opinion he has been right in his resistance and his critics have been shamefully wrong. Over the past three years we have been deluged with half truths, misinformation, and contradiction.
Only this afternoon we listened to the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North (Mr. Coates) suggest that older people who have never collected unemployment insurance should get some kind of claim when they retire. This seems to me to be a view difficult to sustain bearing in mind the fact that many members of his party believe the scheme should be operated on an actuarial basis.
I am afraid the contradictions which emerge from the opposition on this subject of unemployment insurance defy imagination. If one had the time and inclination to go back over the past three years and examine the speeches and comments made by members of the official opposition on this question, one would be here for a long time listing in a column on the left the names of those who are advocating something, and in a column on the right, those who say exactly the opposite. For three years we have been listening to Conservative arguments which would have been appropriate and which, I am sure, were used to defend things like child labour in England in the 19th century.
To hear the kind of argument used the other day by the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) to the effect that industries in his area have to compete not only with the labour market but with the unemployment insurance fund, and that this is a bad thing, shocks me. It shocks me he should suggest such a thing-that people in his area should work for wages which are as low as the kind of payments made by the Unemployment Insurance Commission. As far as I am concerned, industry in his area should have to pay decent wages-wages on which people can live.
I am tired of hearing unemployment insurance whipped as an excuse for paying low wages, and that really is the sense of the arguments we have heard in the last three years-that it is a disincentive to work if you are not going to be paid decent wages. I accept that kind of disincentive. For the information of members who are of that persuasion I might point out that unemployment insurance is one of the important mechanisms at the disposal of government to raise the minimum wage. After all, as we all know, minimum wages are generally under provincial jurisdiction. One of the things the federal government can do is raise the level of unemployment insurance payments and this, of course, obliges people to pay higher wages in a particular area, and that is a proper thing to do.
There is nothing wrong in telling an employer that if he cannot afford to pay decent wages he should not be in business. That is a fact. One should not excuse one's self by blaming his troubles on unemployment insurance while he soaks up his two or three weeks' winter sunshine in Flori-day, Jamaica, Hawaii or wherever he goes, where he talks about his workers back home whom he is paying insufficient wages. I have heard that many times. I do not accept that argument.

November 3, 1975
Unemployment Insurance Act
The average weekly unemployment payment in Canada in July-and I am sure all members are aware of this-was $82.77 a week. Someone might claim that is a disincentive to work. I just have to laugh.
Among the attempts to dilute the unemployment insurance plan, as I read through last week's Hansard, are repeated references to the work ethic. My good friend, the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), referred to it in his speech. The hon. member for Calgary Centre (Mr. Andre) and several others had something to say about the work ethic.
It is positively peculiar to me the way people throw around the expression "the work ethic". Evidently if one works long hours for low wages he has a good work ethic. However, if a person resists and says, "Just a minute; I would like to be paid reasonably well so I can live, or I will go home", then he has a bad work ethic. I am afraid I do not buy that. That is one of the old chestnuts that has been used since 1850.
Personally I have faith in Canadians. Most Canadians do want to work but they want to receive some of the great incentive, money. I know what I am talking about. During the 1950's I worked in the mines. I also spent some years working in the various camps across Canada. I remember Moak Lake, Manitoba in 1956. I was among the first people to sink a shaft at a settlement which I believe now elects a member of parliament. There were 32 of us in the bush. We worked 12 hours a day, 7 days a week, for a period of six months without a day off. Why did we do this? Because we were paid money. The best incentive is money.
I was brought up in the retail business which is notorious for low wages. It is the worst paying industry in the country. When I was going to school I would go out to the camps in the summer and then, when I left school at age 16, I started going around to the various camps to make some money. I worked long hours in the bush in order to pay for my various activities.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Explain!

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Before I came to parliament I worked 12 to 14 hours a day in Toronto in the cab business. I did this for five years before I came to Ottawa. I scraped the streets, like everybody who works at night in Toronto, for every dime. When people such as members opposite speak to me about the work ethic this makes me laugh. I have seen too many people in my day abused by such a cheap cliche as "he does not understand the work ethic". Well, I have been around enough and I am old enough to know a lot of baloney when I hear it.
Decent unemployment insurance is expensive in a time of high unemployment. Of course it is expensive in a time of high unemployment. If it is doing its job of cushioning those who are out of work it must be expensive. In his remarks last Monday the hon. member for Hamilton West noted that the United States, with a population ten times that of Canada, spent $4 billion on unemployment insurance in 1973. He went on to say that we in Canada will spend approximately the same amount in that area in 1975.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: There is something wrong somewhere.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
What is wrong is that in the United States there is a lousy unemployment insurance program. Everybody knows that. In Detroit where there is high unemployment in the automotive industry anyone who can read the newspaper knows the unions are very concerned about the fact that they do not have the kind of unemployment insurance program we enjoy in Canada. Our program is better than theirs.
Canada is an advanced country in the field of unemployment insurance, and the United States is not. With the current recession that is taking place in that country they are very concerned about this.
I would like to point out to hon. members that money spent on unemployment insurance-and people seem to be very concerned about the money spent-does not disappear like smoke. It goes into the local economies. Not only does it put bread on the table but in fact in some of the local communities in parts of Canada which have a consistently high rate of unemployment of 20 per cent or 25 per cent having this kind of money going into their economies is a good thing. I find it difficult to understand a party, some of whose members I regret to say come from those areas of high unemployment, that would say we are spending too much money in those economies. I would like to see those people go back home and tell their people that we are spending too much money in their local economies.
I am against anyone cheating in respect of the unemployment insurance fund, committing fraud, and so on. No sensible person would be in favour of this, and of course it must be stopped wherever possible. Of course the unemployment insurance program should not be abused. It must be reformed and brought up to date, but I want to say I really, genuinely support the minister in his resistance to those who would dilute the unemployment insurance program.
I think it should be made clear to the Canadian working people that there are people in parliament who really would dilute the unemployment insurance program so that it would bear a pale resemblance to what we have today, and would in fact put the clock back. I think the people of Canada should be told that because it is true.
There is a problem in respect of people who cheat the unemployment insurance program, but I am not convinced there is a great number involved. Since the changes made about 18 months ago the regulations in respect of unemployment insurance have been as tight as I would like to see them. I wonder whether in some areas perhaps they are not too tight.
I wish to take this opportunity to explain that there are people who really do not believe there should be proper support for working Canadian men and women who, for reasons beyond their control, find themselves without a decent job. I think that is very important. If people are ripping off the unemployment insurance fund not only is this bad because of the manner in which they are taking the money, but it is particularly bad because it gives the unemployment insurance program a bad name. I do not like that because, as I said, I think unemployment insurance is a very good program.

I have a particular proposal to make regarding sickness benefits under the unemployment insurance program. I do not think the difference between a major attachment period and a minor attachment period is made clear enough to the working person, and I think there is entirely too much jargon in this business.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I myself find it difficult to understand sometimes; I have to refresh my mind continually, and I am sure other hon. members have the same problem. I hope that something can be done to explain this program to the people. I notice there are two kinds of attachment period. My disagreement with this program is that very few people know that during the major contribution period if you become sick, even if you have been collecting sickness benefits for 10 or 15 weeks you are not eligible for unemployment insurance after the fifteenth week. I find it reprehensible that most people do not know that at the end of 15 weeks their sickness benefits cease and, if a person happens to be sick in the sixteenth week, he is not eligible for unemployment insurance. I certainly did not know that and I am sure most Canadians do not realize it.
We all have our favourite unemployment insurance case, and although the Unemployment Insurance Commission in my area does a fair job I also have my horror case, that of a man about 65 years of age, a leather worker who was laid off. He was collecting his unemployment insurance and in the twentieth week he was taken seriously ill, went to hospital and had one lung removed. Naturally he was not reporting to the unemployment insurance office as being available for work.
When he came out of the hospital some time after he had collected his payments and cashed them-I do not think he quite realized what he was doing-he was presented with a bill for $450 to be paid back to unemployment insurance. I think that is dreadful and it is something which should be changed. We have made amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act and it is time we took a look at this byzantine business of sickness benefits because it is not satisfactory. I am sure I am not the only member with cases of people who have been sick and genuinely did not realize they were doing something wrong because they thought they were entitled to unemployment insurance.
When the plan was first announced, sickness benefits were announced with the plan. Why would anybody think he was not entitled to collect unemployment insurance? I personally cannot imagine why. Whenever I see one of these cases it infuriates me, particularly when almost every one of them must return the payment, whether it is $300, $400, or $500. Usually they do not have money and they have to make payments of $4 or $5 a week for the next five years. I think it is an inequity which should be repaired. Something should be done about it.
I see the minister in the House tonight. I merely wanted to use this opportunity to point out to him, first, that people do not understand the difference between a major and minor contribution period-nobody except an actuary understands it, and most of us are not in the insurance business-and second, that there is no consistency in the
Adjournment Debate
program when people who are unemployed become sick and suddenly are cut off unemployment insurance, and wind up owing the government money at a time when they can least afford it.
I would like to make one more point to those who talk about the cost of unemployment insurance. As the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) repeatedly said during the negotiations which have been going on ad nauseam over the last three years, if we want to cut the cost of unemployment insurance the best way is to reduce the number of people who are unemployed.

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ACT (1971) MEASURE TO ADD NEW CLASS OF INSURABLE EMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have the floor for just one minute before ten o'clock because I want to say to the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Stollery), who spoke a moment ago, that for a moment he sounded like the only man who had ever worked for a living. I would never denigrate any other member with regard to his work experience or any other personal effort he might have made, but it has been my experience that those who work hardest talk about it the least. May I call it ten o'clock, Madam Speaker?

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF STAFF-EFFECT ON IMPLEMENTATION OF BILINGUALISM PROGRAM

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF STAFF-EFFECT ON IMPLEMENTATION OF BILINGUALISM PROGRAM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, on October 14, 1975, as recorded at page 8103 of Hansard of that day, I asked the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) whether, as a result of the Prime Minister's (Mr. Trudeau) trip to Damascus on Thanksgiving evening when he ate crow, feathers and all, instead of turkey, the government intended its restraint program to mean and include that it was not proceeding with phase II of the implementation of bilingualism in the public service of Canada.
The minister indicated it meant no such thing, that restraint would not stand in the way of phase II dealing with units working in French and it would be proceeding full speed ahead. If that was not enough, he said that I supported phase II as envisaged by the government. This is just patent nonsense. Phase II deals with units working in French. The government proposes a quota system, 10 per cent of supervisory positions for some departments, 20 per cent for others.
There is no provision in the resolution of June, 1973, dealing with quotas. The words used in that declaration are "where practical", not a quota system. The resolution says that the staff associations would be consulted. No only were they not consulted, their walkout of the National Joint Council in protest of the arrangement proposed

November 3, 1975
Adjournment Debate
indicated they were hoodwinked, and the government had better come clean with them.
There is a very suspicious press release which alludes to some kind of detente within the National Joint Council. It came out on the weekend, with no telephone number for verification or questions. The question I have is who authorized it, who was there, and what does it mean? This question has affected others.
Geoffrey Johnson writing in the Citizen last week said that:
-as a result of receiving certain documents concerning the language program and the facts are simply that beneath the surface of that "agreement", announced last Monday by the public service's National Joint Council on Bilingualism, things are far from well.
The staff side of the council, in fact, is said to be having second thoughts about the whole thing now that the fine print has yielded information on what lies in store for the Anglophone who wants to remain in his job even when it becomes part of a unit working in French.
Treasury Board had backed down to a certain extent by agreeing to provide French-language training for those Anglophones affected.
Now the staff side has discovered to its dismay that these employees will have no chance whatsoever of promotion because they will never qualify linguistically for French-essential positions. Their choice will be to stay put-or get out.
Apparently things have ground to a halt on that point. It's an embarrassing situation for Claude Edwards, president of the Public Service Alliance, and Des Davidge, vice-chairman of the staff side of the council. They were the ones who gave their blessing to the revised agreement on the weekend-without reaching the agreement.
In other words, it seems that despite the statements to the press by the President of the Treasury Board, and despite the soothing syrup of the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Francis) there are grave suspicions, and indeed reports that the situation remains exactly the same today as it did on September 3, 1975, when I revealed the secret documents. I think it is just about time the government came clean.
I have asked the minister for a statement inside the House; he has not given it. He has made some references outside the House, but I suggest that his references are double talk, and it is about time we had the straight goods on this program.
The other matter is the question of merit. I want to say that this policy is about as far removed from merit as the President of the Treasury Board is removed from Thomas D'Arcy McGee.
Phase II is not the program I voted for in June of 1973, and the fact that it is going ahead is the best indication I know of that the restraint program of the government in terms of government spending is about as genuine as a three dollar bill. No one has to prove his allegiance to the principles of the Official Languages Act by refraining from pointing out the inequities and the stupidities in their implementation. Phase II is wrong in principle, it is demoralizing, divisive, discriminatory, and it is contrary to the provisions of the statute which was meant to promote unity in the public service, and unity in this country.
I think it is about time we heard the truth about this program. This program was brought forth by the President of the Treasury Board, in the month of August, not by accident, but because the House was not sitting. There has

been no statement made about it in the House, merely statements outside, and we have heard nothing but the empty statements of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Sharp) a few days ago. There has been a disturbing lack of candor about it which leads me to say that the public service of this country deserves better treatment.
I released those documents after some heart searching, and it is interesting to note that when I released them the President of the Treasury Board said they were nothing. In fact he described them as garbage, but all the while since that time the same President of the Treasury Board and others in the public service have been discussing that which was supposed to be nothing and which was described as garbage.
I think the parliamentary secretary had better come clean tonight. What is his position? What is the position of the Government of Canada with respect to this matter? Has phase II stopped? Is phase II being changed? If so, to what extent? How is the discrimination being taken out of it? Those are the questions being asked by the public service of this country and, as I said earlier, I believe that the public service of this country deserves some candor in terms of this very important program.
