speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-PROPOSED REDUCTION OF STAFF-EFFECT ON IMPLEMENTATION OF BILINGUALISM PROGRAM
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, at present implementation of all elements of Part II of the official languages program is under renewed discussion with heads of bargaining agents. I say renewed because there was a breakdown in the consultation process, to which the hon. member referred. I believe that the frank and open discussions which have already taken place, and those continuing now, will result in the resolution of many, hopefully all, of the concerns of the bargaining agents. These discussions, as I said, are taking place on a continuing basis.
As the implementation of phase II is presently the subject of discussion with the National-Joint Council, I do not want to prejudge the outcome of these discussions. Without question, the hon. member raised a number of important points. I merely wish to emphasize that the position of the government is that of complete equality for the two official languages. This policy will be implemented in connection with the proposals. Any aspects which involve discrimination between language groups, and access to units working in French, will be eliminated. The opportunities for promotion within those units will be there to those who meet proficiency requirements, no matter what is their mother tongue.

subtopic: POST OFFICE-PROPOSAL TO ALLOW PRIVATE CARRIERS TO DELIVER MAIL-GOVERNMENT POSITION
POST OFFICE-PROPOSAL TO ALLOW PRIVATE CARRIERS TO DELIVER MAIL-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I certainly hope I shall receive a better answer than that given to the previous hon. member.
On October 23 I asked the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) to indicate, as recorded on page 8477 of Hansard:
... if he has any plans to allow private carriers to deliver first class mail, any other sort of mail or parcels during the Post Office strike, and would he consider initiating discussions with the Air Industries Asso-

ciation and the Canadian Truckers Association, to assure that the fullest possible use is made of alternative delivery services in the absence of regular postal service.
I pointed out to the minister that I had spoken with these groups earlier that day and that they would be willing to sit down with the hon. gentleman to discuss alternate ways of delivering mail. To this the Postmaster General replied, in part:
I am aware of the representations but I think it is a little premature to be encouraging our competition.
This thinking on the part of the Postmaster General, that private couriers are competition, must be stopped. To make my position perfectly clear, let me say that I am waiting for the Postmaster General to begin consultations with the private sector on rates and sorting problems, with a view to transferring as much mail delivery as possible to trucking and airline firms and private couriers.
I have raised this subject previously in the House, but the answers were entirely unsatisfactory. One of the reasons given for refusal was that private carriers would not deliver mail or parcels to remote areas. I point out that regional air carriers and trucking companies deliver merchandise to remote areas of Canada. So why could they not deliver mail as well? One of the answers I received earlier was that a private mail carrier would not deliver a letter to the north pole. That is an absolutely ridiculous answer. Our remote cities, towns, and villages all need mail service; the odd remote area might suffer a little. But we cannot use that as an excuse for not doing something to ensure proper mail delivery in Canada.
As announced today, Montreal postal workers are forming a courier delivery service. I suggest that they should also negotiate with the trucking and airline associations to work out long-range plans for postal delivery. I am sure they would be much happier working for a private concern instead of being out on strike all the time, which is what happens to those working for our postal service in Canada.
The direct mail industry is considering its own mail delivery service, as it has been crippled 38 times in past few years owing to post office strikes. Canada's direct mail and mail order industry is considering setting up its own delivery service for second and third class mail. A similar service in the United States pays better wages than the post office, is cheaper, and is more efficient, they say. The U.S. service, United Parcel Service, tried to enter Canada in recent months but its application to the Foreign Investment Review Agency to buy two Canadian delivery services was rejected. That is most unfortunate. I suggest to the unions that they should also consider consulting with private carriers. If they could make higher wages and not be out on strike all the time, everybody would benefit.
Recently the Postmaster General stated that Canada's Post Office must regain the confidence of the public, provide better facilities for its employees, and go after the
3,000	jobs that were lost because of work stoppages and strikes by postal workers. That statement was made in August. If there were 3,000 jobs lost last August, heaven only knows how many jobs have been lost with this latest strike.
Adjournment Debate
Businesses large and small cannot go on year after year waiting for the Postmaster General to provide better service. The business that has been lost to the private couriers will never be regained by the post office, so let us negotiate to transfer the remaining delivery to the private sector. The government has a responsibility to provide guaranteed postal delivery for Canadians.
Here is an example of what is happening to some Canadians firms. Strikes are crippling mail order firms. A Cornwall mail order company may be forced to lay off 300 employees as a result of strikes by inside postal workers. Jack MacDonald, president of Sovereign Seat Covers Manufacturing Limited, said that the company, which relies totally on mail orders, has been hit hard by the postal strike. He said, and I quote:
Our situation would be that as soon as our... 48-hour work backlog is cleaned up we will have about 300 employees with nothing to do.
That is only one firm. There are dozens of others across the country that are faced with the same situation. This is what the latest strike is doing to postal business in the United States. I quote:
Montrealers frustrated at the Canadian postal strike are driving to U.S. border points to drop off correspondence for the United States and other foreign destinations. This northern New York city, 70 miles south of Montreal, has developed a booming postal business since the strike began, giving extra revenue to the U.S. Treasury and overtime work to postal employees. Last Thursday, 184,000 pieces of mail were processed in the Plattsburgh post office, an increase of about 16,000 compared with the previous Thursday, said city postmaster Rolland Hewitt.
That mail should be hosted in this country. That is why I suggest that the Postmaster General start immediate negotiations with the private sector to keep these 184,000 pieces of mail in Canada rather than give the revenue to American firms.
What we are faced with today is a number of ad hoc schemes to deliver mail. A concerned gentleman in Victoria has formed a postal delivery service. He has some striking post office workers helping him deliver the mail. It is absolutely ridiculous for a country the size of Canada to be faced with this sort of situation. Many hon. members will have seen the headline: "Halifax Posties Set Up Delivery System". They are trying to do something there.
The Postmaster General stated recently that illegal work stoppages by postal employees posed a threat to their job security by encouraging private carriers to compete with the government. Private carriers, he said, would get a toe hold only because of labour unrest and the uncertainty of moving the mail.

Madam Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. McKenzie) for his suggestion. There is no doubt that a long postal strike would be most disruptive to the Canadian people generally, to the Canadian economy, and to businesses both large and small. As the hon. member has indicated, a strike even of the present duration has taken its toll. Should it last much longer, alternate means will certainly be forthcoming to deal with essential mail.

November 3, 1975
Adjournment Debate
However, it should be remembered that members of the Canadian Union of Postal Workers are exercising their democratic right in walking off their jobs, and in a democratic society such as ours we must be ready to accept the hardships and inconveniences brought about by this exercise of the democratic process. At this moment the government is hopeful of an early settlement to the strike. The difficulties we are facing with the Canadian postal workers are difficulties which have been experienced over a long period and they have been the cause of many walkouts. It is hoped that the successful completion of these negotiations, carefully put, together will create a better relationship and that walk-outs of the kind we have known will cease.
As of 6.30 this evening agreement had been reached on all but two of the outstanding issues-pay, and the employment of casuals. It is hoped that within a short period agreement will be reached and that the development of alternative means of delivering mail will, consequently, not be required.

subtopic: BROADCASTING-ACTIONS OF UNITED STATES TELEVISION STATIONS IN OBTAINING CANADIAN ADVERTISING-GOVERNMENT ACTION
BROADCASTING-ACTIONS OF UNITED STATES TELEVISION STATIONS IN OBTAINING CANADIAN ADVERTISING-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I raised a question with the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) concerning a practice which has been going on since last spring, namely, the dumping of advertising space by United States border television stations on the Canadian market.
Before the House is Bill C-58, a belated recognition by the Liberal government of the crisis in the Canadian communications industry-magazines and television. The purpose of that bill is to help the Canadian magazine and television industries by making amendments to the Income Tax Act so that we may enhance our own national identity and have Canadians interpret the events of the world to other Canadians rather than relying on foreign magazines and news sources. What we have experienced, unfortunately, is delay in the passage of this bill mainly due to a filibuster mounted by the Conservative party.
In the intervening period, many United States border television stations are adopting punitive and retaliatory measures consequent upon the introduction of this bill although it has yet to be passed and made law. Specifically what they are doing is dumping advertising slots on Canadian advertisers only. They are dumping advertising space at cut rates to under sell Canadian stations and force them into a loss position. This practice can only be viewed as punitive and retaliatory. It particularly hurts the smaller independent stations along our border.
For example, in the fall of 1974 a Buffalo television station was charging between $60 and $80 for a rating point-that is the terminology used in selling advertising. By the spring of 1975 the same station was charging only $22 per rating point on the Canadian side only. This fall the rate has risen to $30, still approximately half the normal advertising rate charged by the station to its American customers, and about half the rate in Canada. Many Canadian stations barely get by when they sell these rating points at between $40 and $45. For example, City TV

in Toronto has estimated that in one eight week period alone it lost over $200,000 in advertising contracts because of this practice on the part of U.S. border stations.
We also find dumping taking place on the west side of Canada. There is a certain station, KVOS, in Bellingham, Washington, which has been set up purely to take advantage of Canadian business-there is not enough American business in this area to make its operation viable otherwise. Last June this station sold 104-week contracts at a rating point of $30, with a $600 a month minimum contract. In addition, KVOS has given Canadian advertisers a guarantee that when the income tax provisions of Bill C-58 come into effect those advertisers will be offered a rate cut by a further 50 per cent.
It has been estimated that, in 12 deals sold by that one station alone in Washington in a period of one week, they were able to capture contracts from Canadian advertisers amounting to some $4 million. That is $4 million worth of Canadian advertising revenue for one station alone, money that went to the United States rather than remain in Canada to help support Canadian television stations.
The question may be raised: how can these American stations afford such cut rate prices for advertising? The reason is that the United States stations along the border make more than an adequate profit on the United States market alone. For example, the Buffalo station has a 150 per cent return on equity investment, not counting its Canadian business. Therefore any advertising sold in the Canadian market is pure gravy. It is surplus to the actual needs of any American television station.
This problem was brought to the attention of the then minister of finance last spring, the minister of communications, and the chairman of the CRTC during the summer. They were aware of the problem, but nothing to date has been done. Since the effect of the tax provisions in Bill C-58 is to double the cost of advertising spots placed by Canadian advertisers on United States television, all a U.S. television station has to do to circumvent the legislation is to cut its rates to advertisers on the Canadian side by 51 per cent or more. Therefore the whole intent of the legislation will be negated.
My question to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State (Miss Campbell) is: will the government be taking measures to overcome this obvious weakness in Bill C-58? Will the minister bring forward amendments to plug the loopholes in this legislation? Specifically I suggest a double disallowance feature, that is to say, to disallow as a normal business expense for tax purposes twice the value of advertising spots on United States television stations. That would get around the effect of their cutting their rates.
I also want to know whether the minister will take immediate steps under the anti-dumping legislation via order in council to stop this undercutting of revenue for Canadian stations. In conclusion I want to make th* point that, unless action is taken now, this punitive dumping tactic of American television stations will undermine the financial viability of many Canadian television stations and their ability to produce Canadian programs.
November 3, 1975

speakeroldname: Miss Coline Campbell (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: BROADCASTING-ACTIONS OF UNITED STATES TELEVISION STATIONS IN OBTAINING CANADIAN ADVERTISING-GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in the absence of the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications (Mr. Fleming) I would like to reaffirm that the government introduced in Bill C-58 an amendment to the Income Tax Act which would no longer allow deductions against income for advertising time on a non-Canadian station for advertisements directed primarily to a Canadian market. The purpose of the amendment is to constrain the significant outflow, estimated at some $20 million a year, by Canadian firms purchasing advertisement time on United States border stations.
Adjournment Debate
The government is aware of possible alternatives which United States border stations might offer to Canadian advertisers as an incentive to maintain their business. As the legislation has yet to be passed, it is much too early to judge the effects of Bill C-58.
The Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) stated in the House this afternoon that it is considered that the remedy to the situation alluded to by the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) lies in a speedy passage of Bill C-58. It should also be remembered that U.S. border stations are not exporting goods but providing services, and that therefore it would seem that the anti-dumping act would not apply as it is now written.
